areas.name: How LLMs run
areas.why: Every cost and delay in AI infrastructure traces back to how a model reads memory and uses the GPU. This is the base everything else stands on.

areas.name: Measuring things
areas.why: You cannot fix or buy what you cannot measure. Most bad infra decisions come from a benchmark nobody questioned.

areas.name: Scheduling & control planes
areas.why: A cluster is only useful if the right job lands on the right GPUs and stays healthy. This is the software that decides.

areas.name: Failure & state
areas.why: Machines die and messages repeat. Anything that handles money, jobs or data has to stay correct anyway.

areas.name: Linux & isolation
areas.why: Running code you do not trust is only safe if you know what the operating system can and cannot wall off.

areas.name: Agents & evals
areas.why: Agents run code a model wrote, and evals judge models. Both need walls around the code and honest statistics.

areas.name: Leading agents
areas.why: Most of the work will be done by agents. The skill is deciding what to build, writing specs agents can follow, checking their work, and staying the human in the loop who owns the decisions.

areas.name: AI safety & security
areas.why: Models and agents can be tricked, misused or leaked. This is the engineering that keeps them contained, watched and recoverable. It builds on isolation, evals and observability.

areas.name: GPU fleets & training
areas.why: With thousands of GPUs, hardware failure is normal. This is how long jobs and big fleets stay healthy and changes roll out safely.

areas.name: Using AI day to day
areas.why: A year-long thread: use AI tools every day while you learn how they work, with one small build per phase.

areas.name: Data structures and algorithms
areas.why: Coding rounds test a small set of patterns. Each topic here is one pattern family with its practice problems; working the problems is how the pattern is learned.

areas.name: System design
areas.why: A design round tests whether you can pick the right building blocks for a given scale. Each topic here is one building block or system family, with the design items that practise it.

phases.name: Measure before you optimise
phases.idea: Decoding re-reads every weight for each token, so memory speed is the limit. Waiting lines blow up near full load. A benchmark is an instrument with error.

phases.name: Batching, KV cache, parallelism, Go
phases.idea: The KV cache is memory you page, share and evict. The batch is the scheduler. Splitting a model over GPUs trades memory for communication.

phases.name: The control plane
phases.idea: Placement is packing under topology and gang rules. A controller is a reconcile loop with honest status. Scale on queue depth and KV pressure, not GPU utilisation.

phases.name: State, failure, data movement
phases.idea: Assume every call can fail, repeat, reorder or hang. Correctness comes from idempotency, invariants and recovery.

phases.name: Isolation, agents, evals
phases.idea: Untrusted code needs a smaller trusted base. An agent harness is a loop plus permissions plus a journal. An eval score is a noisy measurement of a noisy system.

phases.name: GPU fleets, training, safe rollout
phases.idea: At fleet scale hardware failure is routine. Node health is a state machine. Every change is gated by evidence.

nodes.title: Neural network basics
nodes.oneLiner: A neural network turns numbers into other numbers using adjustable values called weights.
nodes.why: Every later idea (why a model is big, why it needs GPU memory) rests on this picture.
explain: What is a weight, and why does a bigger model need more memory?

nodes.title: Transformers and attention
nodes.oneLiner: A transformer reads text as tokens (word pieces) and uses attention to decide which earlier tokens matter for the next one.
nodes.why: The KV cache, batching and most serving tricks exist because of how attention works.
explain: What does attention look at when the model picks the next token?
Why does a longer prompt cost more?

nodes.title: The LLM lifecycle: tokens, pretraining, post-training
nodes.short: How an LLM is made · 3 h
nodes.oneLiner: From raw text to a chat model: split text into tokens, pretrain on huge text, fine-tune, apply reinforcement learning, then sample answers.
nodes.why: You will host, tune and evaluate these models, so you need to know what each stage produces and what it costs.
explain: Why does a reasoning model cost more to serve than a chat model for the same question?
What does RLHF add after supervised fine-tuning, and why does an infra engineer care?

nodes.title: Inference concepts: prefill, decode, KV cache, batching
nodes.oneLiner: Serving a model has two steps: read the whole prompt at once (prefill), then produce one token at a time (decode).
nodes.why: This is the job itself. Prefill and decode stress different parts of the GPU.
explain: Why is decode slow even on a fast GPU?
What is the KV cache (key-value cache) saving?

nodes.title: GPU memory arithmetic
nodes.oneLiner: Add up the weights plus the KV cache and compare the total with the GPU's memory.
nodes.why: The one skill you must be able to do on paper: will this model fit, and how many users at once?
explain: Will a 70-billion-parameter model fit on one 80 GB GPU with 16-bit numbers? Show the sum.

nodes.title: Touch the real thing: run a small model locally, plus a free-tier vLLM run
nodes.oneLiner: Run a small model on your laptop, then run vLLM (an open-source model server) once on a free Modal or Kaggle GPU.
nodes.why: Seeing real tokens arrive and real memory fill up makes the later simulations feel earned instead of abstract.
explain: How many tokens per second did you get, and what limited it?

nodes.title: Memory and compute bounds of LLM inference
nodes.oneLiner: Prefill is limited by compute. Decode is limited by how fast the GPU can read its weights.
nodes.why: It explains almost every serving decision: why batching helps, why long prompts hurt, why big GPUs have fast memory.
explain: Why is decode memory-bound while prefill is compute-bound?
What does a roofline chart tell you that a profiler does not?

nodes.title: tokensim (Python)
nodes.oneLiner: A simulated LLM engine with a load generator and a fake OpenAI-style server. You sweep the load and watch latency blow up where the maths says it should.
nodes.why: The first build. It forces you to put numbers on memory limits, queues and benchmarks.
explain: Why does the latency curve have a knee, and where is it?

nodes.title: Touch the real thing: vLLM prefix caching on a cheap rented GPU
nodes.oneLiner: Rent a cheap GPU for a few hours and run vLLM with prefix caching on and off, changing batch size and quantisation.
nodes.why: You see what the KV cache does on real hardware before you build your own.
explain: What changed in time to first token when prefix caching turned on?

nodes.title: Continuous batching and KV-cache management
nodes.oneLiner: The server keeps a running batch, adds new requests at every step, and stores each request's attention memory (the KV cache) in blocks.
nodes.why: KV-cache memory decides how many users fit on one GPU.
explain: What is paged attention and why does it exist?
When does prefix caching help, and when does it hurt?

nodes.title: Parallelism (tensor, pipeline, expert, data) and its communication cost
nodes.oneLiner: Split a model over several GPUs and pay for it with communication between them.
nodes.why: Models too big for one GPU force this, and it is the reason serving needs gang scheduling later.
explain: Why can more GPUs with tensor parallelism lower per-GPU throughput?

nodes.title: Quantisation and speculative decoding
nodes.oneLiner: Use smaller numbers, or guess ahead with a small model, to trade a little quality for speed.
nodes.why: Know the trade so you can read a vendor's claims critically.
explain: What do you give up when you quantise a model to 4 bits?

nodes.title: Serving engines in practice (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM)
nodes.oneLiner: Know what the main open-source model servers are and what each is good at.
nodes.why: Job posts name them, but the ideas underneath matter more. One short unit is enough.
explain: What problem did vLLM solve that made it popular?

nodes.title: GPU architecture and kernel authoring tour
nodes.oneLiner: A read-level tour of how a GPU is built and what a kernel (a small GPU program) is.
nodes.why: Lets you follow specialist conversations without writing kernels yourself.
explain: Why are GPU memory and compute separate bottlenecks?

nodes.title: kvlab (Go)
nodes.oneLiner: A paged KV-cache block allocator with prefix sharing and eviction, tested against a simple reference model.
nodes.why: Turns the KV cache from a diagram into code you can break.
explain: How do you prove the allocator never leaks or double-frees a block?

nodes.title: Benchmarking and measurement method
nodes.oneLiner: Treat a benchmark as an instrument: fixed load, a warm-up, repeats and an error bar.
nodes.why: Goodput (useful requests per second that meet the latency target) beats raw throughput, and you only see that if you measure properly.
explain: How do you benchmark an LLM endpoint fairly?
What is goodput and why does it beat throughput?

nodes.title: Queueing theory and tail latency
nodes.oneLiner: When a system is nearly full, waiting lines explode and the slowest requests (p99, the 99th percentile) get far worse than the average.
nodes.why: It tells you why a service at 85% load feels broken, and it is the basis of autoscaling and capacity planning.
explain: Why does p99 explode near 85% utilisation?
What does Little's law say, in one sentence?

nodes.title: Performance profiling method
nodes.oneLiner: Find the real bottleneck by measuring, not guessing: CPU, memory, GPU or network.
nodes.why: The habit transfers to every system you will touch.
explain: How do you tell whether a slow request is waiting or working?

nodes.title: Observability for LLM and agent systems
nodes.oneLiner: Traces, metrics and logs that show what a model call or agent step did and what it cost.
nodes.why: Marked maintain: it builds on observability you already use, adding model-specific traces.
explain: What would you want in a trace of one agent step?

nodes.title: Capacity planning and unit economics ($ per token)
nodes.oneLiner: Work out how many GPUs you need and what each million tokens costs.
nodes.why: It joins your measurements, your ledger and your queueing maths into the number the business asks for.
explain: How do you find idle GPUs and compute the cost per million tokens?

nodes.title: Go systems programming
nodes.oneLiner: A small, fast language used for most Kubernetes and infrastructure tools.
nodes.why: Controllers and nearly every build from here on are written in Go.
explain: How do goroutines and channels differ from threads and locks?

nodes.title: Touch the real thing: install Kueue on kind and queue a real gang of pods
nodes.oneLiner: Install Kueue (a job-queue add-on for Kubernetes) on a local kind cluster and submit a group of pods that must start together.
nodes.why: You watch a real scheduler hold a job back until every pod in it can fit.
explain: What happened to the job while only some of its pods could fit?

nodes.title: Scheduling and bin-packing (gang, topology, preemption, fair share)
nodes.oneLiner: Choosing which job runs on which machines, like packing a suitcase where some items must travel together.
nodes.why: Idle GPUs are the most expensive waste in AI infrastructure. Good placement is the fix.
explain: Why does a replica split over 8 GPUs need gang scheduling?
What can a bin-packer do that the default Kubernetes scheduler cannot?

nodes.title: Kubernetes controllers and CRDs in Go
nodes.oneLiner: A controller keeps watching the cluster and nudges it toward the state you declared. A CRD (custom resource definition) adds your own object type.
nodes.why: This is how a model deployment becomes one more Kubernetes object that heals itself.
explain: Why must a controller be level-triggered rather than event-triggered?

nodes.title: Routing, gateways and fairness for cached backends
nodes.oneLiner: Send each request to the replica most likely to already hold its prefix in cache, without overloading that replica.
nodes.why: Cache-aware routing can cut cost a lot, but a hot prefix can overload a single replica.
explain: How do you route for cache hits without hot-spotting one replica?

nodes.title: Autoscaling on the right signal; cold start and weight distribution
nodes.oneLiner: Add or remove replicas based on queue depth and KV-cache pressure, not GPU utilisation.
nodes.why: GPU utilisation looks busy even when the queue is empty, so it scales too late or too early. A new replica also has to copy tens of gigabytes of weights.
explain: Why not autoscale on GPU utilisation?
What makes a cold start slow?

nodes.title: Accelerator resource model (device plugin, DRA, MIG)
nodes.oneLiner: How Kubernetes learns what GPUs exist: device plugins, DRA (dynamic resource allocation) and MIG (slicing one GPU into parts).
nodes.why: Rarely named in job posts today, so one short unit is enough to know it exists.
explain: What does a device plugin tell the scheduler?

nodes.title: LeaderWorkerSet: gang-scheduled multi-pod serving
nodes.oneLiner: A Kubernetes object that runs one model replica as a group of pods (one leader, several workers) that start, fail and restart together.
nodes.why: Models that span several machines need exactly this. You try it on a kind cluster with fake GPUs, so no rental is needed.
explain: What goes wrong if one worker pod of a multi-pod replica restarts alone?

nodes.title: fleetd (Go, kind)
nodes.oneLiner: A ModelDeployment controller, gang-aware placement, a KV-aware router and a queue-depth autoscaler, driving the fake engines.
nodes.why: The first build that behaves like a real platform.
explain: What should the status say when a replica is not attempted, failed or degraded?

nodes.title: Infrastructure as code, cloud, CI/CD
nodes.oneLiner: Terraform, cloud accounts and pipelines that ship the changes you gate.
nodes.why: Marked maintain: widely requested, and you reach for it while delivering the fleet.
explain: What should a pipeline check before it touches a production cluster?

nodes.title: Touch the real thing: kill a real Postgres mid-write and time a real weights download
nodes.oneLiner: Run a real Postgres, kill it with kill -9 in the middle of a write, and time how long a multi-gigabyte model download takes over a throttled network.
nodes.why: Failure becomes something you watched happen, not just read about.
explain: What state was the database in after the crash?

nodes.title: Failure handling in distributed systems
nodes.oneLiner: Assume every call can fail, repeat, arrive out of order or hang, and design so the result is still correct.
nodes.why: The most requested idea in the job posts, and the base for money, jobs and data. Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as once.
explain: Why is 'exactly once' really at-least-once plus idempotency?

nodes.title: Postgres and database internals
nodes.oneLiner: How a relational database stays correct: transactions, MVCC (multi-version concurrency control), indexes and the write-ahead log.
nodes.why: It is the default home for ledgers, job queues and state.
explain: What does MVCC cost?

nodes.title: Queues, logs and durable execution
nodes.oneLiner: Write the work down before doing it (an outbox or a log) so a crash can pick up where it stopped.
nodes.why: This pattern makes billing, agent journals and eval resumption safe.
explain: What is an outbox and what problem does it solve?

nodes.title: Storage and data movement
nodes.oneLiner: Object stores, caches, and moving very large files quickly.
nodes.why: Weights and checkpoints are huge, so moving them dominates cold starts and recovery.
explain: How do peer caches speed up pulling a 140 GB checkpoint to many replicas?

nodes.title: Metering, quotas and billing as a data problem
nodes.oneLiner: Count the tokens each customer uses exactly once, and enforce limits.
nodes.why: Money makes correctness non-negotiable: the ledger total must equal the tokens actually served.
explain: How do you avoid charging twice when a usage event is retried?

nodes.title: ledger (Go, Postgres)
nodes.oneLiner: LLM-gateway metering and quotas with idempotent usage events, an outbox, and failure injection.
nodes.why: Proves your failure handling works by breaking it on purpose.
explain: How do you check the ledger total equals the tokens served after a crash?

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals
nodes.oneLiner: How packets, TCP, timeouts and load balancers behave when the network is bad.
nodes.why: Token streaming and GPU-to-GPU traffic both depend on it.
explain: Why does packet loss stall token streaming?

nodes.title: Linux internals (cgroups, namespaces, memory, eBPF)
nodes.oneLiner: Cgroups limit what a process can use, namespaces limit what it can see, and eBPF lets you watch the kernel.
nodes.why: Containers and sandboxes are built from exactly these pieces.
explain: What do cgroups limit, and what do namespaces hide?

nodes.title: Touch the real thing: run code in a container and in gVisor and compare
nodes.oneLiner: Run the same code in a plain container and in gVisor (a user-space kernel) and compare what each one can reach.
nodes.why: Isolation stops being theory when you see the difference yourself.
explain: What could the code read in the container that it could not in gVisor?

nodes.title: Isolation and sandboxing (containers, gVisor, microVMs)
nodes.oneLiner: Three ways to wall off untrusted code: containers, gVisor, and microVMs (tiny virtual machines such as Firecracker).
nodes.why: AI agents run code that a model wrote, so the wall has to hold.
explain: Container vs gVisor vs microVM: what does each trade away?

nodes.title: Reading Rust and C++ systems code
nodes.oneLiner: Be able to read the systems code under sandboxes and engines, even if you do not write it.
nodes.why: Firecracker is Rust and many engines are C++, and job posts expect you to follow them.
explain: Where would you look first to see how a sandbox starts?

nodes.title: sandboxd (Go, Linux VM)
nodes.oneLiner: A sandbox runner on rootless containers and gVisor, a small tool-using agent harness with a journal, and an eval runner for 500 tasks.
nodes.why: Brings isolation, agents and evals into one system.
explain: How do you show the sandbox allowed zero escapes?

nodes.title: Agent runtime and harness architecture
nodes.oneLiner: The loop that calls the model, runs tools, checks permissions, and writes a journal so a session can resume.
nodes.why: Harnesses are the product at labs that build coding agents.
explain: How can an agent run code without being able to read secrets?

nodes.title: Evals as measurement systems
nodes.oneLiner: An eval score is a noisy measurement of a noisy system, so report it with error bars.
nodes.why: The same model can score differently on a busy cluster, which changes decisions.
explain: Why does one model score differently on a busy cluster?

nodes.title: Eval and RL-environment infrastructure at scale
nodes.oneLiner: Running 100,000 sandboxed tasks, surviving crashes and resuming without redoing finished work.
nodes.why: Labs run huge numbers of evals and training environments; the infrastructure is the hard part.
explain: How do you run 100,000 sandboxed evals and resume after a crash?

nodes.title: Work with Claude Code daily
nodes.oneLiner: Deliberate practice: hand real tasks from your job to an agent every day, and keep a short log of what worked, what you had to redo and why.
nodes.why: Judgement about agents comes from reps. The log turns vague impressions into a list of what to delegate, what to keep, and how to word a request.
explain: Which task did you delegate this week that you would not delegate again, and why?

nodes.title: Specs agents can follow
nodes.oneLiner: Write a task spec an agent can finish without guessing: the goal, the context it needs, the files it may touch, and acceptance criteria you can check.
nodes.why: An agent does what the spec says, not what you meant. Vague specs give confident work that solves the wrong problem.
explain: What would you add to a one-line request so an agent could not misread it?
What is an acceptance criterion, and how do you make it checkable?

nodes.title: Decompose and delegate
nodes.oneLiner: Split a large piece of work into independent agent tasks, pick a model tier for each (small and cheap for routine edits, large for hard design), and run parallel workers that do not collide.
nodes.why: Parallel agents are only faster if the tasks are independent. The split, and the model choice per task, set both the speed and the bill.
explain: How do you tell whether two tasks are independent enough to run in parallel?
When is a cheaper model the right choice?

nodes.title: Verify agent work
nodes.oneLiner: Treat tests as the sensor: review gates, holdout checks the agent never saw, and a habit of looking for output that is confident but wrong.
nodes.why: Agents report success whether or not it is true. Checking work you did not write is now the main skill, and it uses the same eval thinking as your harness.
explain: What is a holdout check, and why must the agent not see it?
What are the signs of confident-but-wrong output?

nodes.title: Agent budgets and guardrails
nodes.oneLiner: Set token and cost budgets per task, choose the permission mode an agent runs in, and put approval points before anything hard to undo.
nodes.why: An unattended agent can burn money or break things in minutes. Limits you set before the run are cheaper than cleanup after it.
explain: Where in a task would you require a human approval, and why there?
How would you cap what one agent run can spend?

nodes.title: Human in the loop
nodes.oneLiner: Decide which decisions stay with a person, check that agent output still matches what you intended, and know when an agent should stop and escalate.
nodes.why: The agent does the work, but you own the outcome. Drift from your intent is quiet, so you need explicit checks and clear escalation rules.
explain: Which three decisions would you never hand to an agent?
How would you notice that an agent's output has drifted from your intent?

nodes.title: Run your software factory
nodes.oneLiner: Run a ticket-to-PR pipeline on your own side projects, and track cycle time, rework rate and cost per merged change.
nodes.why: It joins the whole area in one working system, and the three numbers show whether the agents are actually helping or just producing more to review.
explain: What does a high rework rate tell you about your specs or your gates?
How do you work out the cost per merged change?

nodes.title: Agent security: prompt injection, the lethal trifecta, least privilege
nodes.oneLiner: Decide what an agent may read, write and reach, and make everything else impossible. Watch for the 'lethal trifecta': private data, untrusted input and a way to send data out, all in one agent.
nodes.why: Prompt injection (text that tries to hijack the agent) is contained by capability design, least-privilege tools and approval gates, not by hoping the model refuses. In the learning map this topic sat under Linux & isolation; it moves here.
explain: What is the lethal trifecta, and which one of its three parts is easiest to remove?
What is prompt injection, and which design limits the damage?

nodes.title: Model weight security
nodes.oneLiner: Protect the model files: tight access control, isolated environments for running them, and controls for insider risk.
nodes.why: Weights are among the most valuable files a lab owns, and they are huge and copied around constantly (see storage and data movement).
explain: Who can read the weights today, and how would you know if someone copied them?

nodes.title: Safety evals at scale (reproducible, sandboxed)
nodes.oneLiner: Run capability and safety test suites (for example the UK AI Security Institute's Inspect framework) inside sandboxes, so results can be repeated.
nodes.why: Some of these tests make the model run risky code, so they need walls, and the scores need to be reproducible to be trusted.
explain: Why must a safety eval run in a sandbox?
How do you know two runs of the same eval are comparable?

nodes.title: Production monitoring of model behaviour
nodes.oneLiner: Watch live traffic for misuse, run safety classifiers (small checking models) next to the main model, and keep an audit log.
nodes.why: You only find out about misuse in production if the gateway that counts usage also records and checks what is asked.
explain: What would you log to investigate a complaint without storing more private data than needed?

nodes.title: Red-teaming infrastructure
nodes.oneLiner: An automated harness that attacks a model or agent with known tricks, and tracks which attacks work over time.
nodes.why: Fixes only stay fixed if every past attack is replayed after each change, like a regression test suite.
explain: How is a red-team regression suite like a normal unit-test suite?

nodes.title: AI incident response: runbooks and kill switches
nodes.oneLiner: Runbooks and a kill switch for when a model or agent misbehaves: how to stop it, limit the damage and learn from it.
nodes.why: Fast containment depends on controls you built before the incident, and on monitoring that notices in time.
explain: What is the fastest safe way to turn off one misbehaving agent without taking down the service?

nodes.title: Fault tolerance for long jobs (checkpoint, goodput)
nodes.oneLiner: Save progress regularly so a dead GPU costs minutes instead of days.
nodes.why: A training run over thousands of GPUs will be interrupted. The checkpoint interval is a cost trade-off (the Young/Daly formula).
explain: What happens when a GPU dies mid-training, and how do you pick a checkpoint interval?

nodes.title: Touch the real thing: distributed training on 2 rented GPUs
nodes.oneLiner: On 2 rented GPUs, run a distributed training job (torchrun with FSDP), kill a worker and resume, run nccl-tests, and read a real DCGM (NVIDIA's GPU health exporter) endpoint.
nodes.why: The only place the plan truly needs real multi-GPU hardware. The map estimates $12 to $25 (unverified).
explain: What changed in the job when you killed a worker?

nodes.title: Distributed training from the infra side
nodes.oneLiner: Running big training jobs reliably: parallelism, checkpoints, restarts and goodput.
nodes.why: You run the job for researchers; you do not design the model.
explain: What does goodput mean for training?

nodes.title: Collectives and network fabrics (NCCL, RDMA/InfiniBand)
nodes.oneLiner: How GPUs share results: all-reduce operations over fast links (NCCL is the library; RDMA is the fast networking).
nodes.why: At scale the network, not the GPU, often sets the speed.
explain: What does ring all-reduce cost as GPUs scale, and why does topology matter?

nodes.title: GPU fleet reliability
nodes.oneLiner: Treat each node's health as a state machine: healthy, suspect, cordoned, draining, repairing.
nodes.why: At fleet scale hardware failure is routine, so the software has to handle it calmly.
explain: How do you tell a bad GPU from a bad job?

nodes.title: Safe rollout and progressive delivery for models and fleets
nodes.oneLiner: Roll a driver or a model across many nodes in waves, with a stop rule and a canary gated by evals.
nodes.why: Every change to a fleet is a risk; the gate turns it into a measured step.
explain: How do you roll a driver across 2,000 nodes safely?

nodes.title: gpufleet (Go, Prometheus)
nodes.oneLiner: A simulated GPU fleet with a node-health controller, eval-gated canary rollouts and cost per million tokens.
nodes.why: The capstone: every earlier build shows up in it.
explain: Why must no rollout wave proceed while nodes remain unattempted?

nodes.title: Small build: a structured-output client with retries
nodes.oneLiner: Write a small client that asks a model for JSON, checks it, and retries when the answer is malformed.
nodes.why: Your first AI-backend piece. It shows quickly why structured output is hard and why retries need care.
explain: What do you do when the model returns almost-valid JSON?

nodes.title: Small build: a tiny RAG app on Postgres
nodes.oneLiner: Build a small retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app: store text as embeddings in Postgres, fetch the closest chunks and hand them to a model.
nodes.why: A first look at the most common AI backend pattern, using a database you will study properly in P4.
explain: What is an embedding, in one sentence?

nodes.title: LLM API engineering (streaming, retries, limits)
nodes.oneLiner: Streaming, retries, rate limits, structured outputs and error handling when you call a model API.
nodes.why: You wrote a client in P1; this names the real patterns underneath it.
explain: Why do streamed responses need different retry rules?

nodes.title: Small build: an MCP server in Go
nodes.oneLiner: Write an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server in Go so an AI assistant can call a tool you built.
nodes.why: You use AI tools every day; now build the other side of the plug, in the language of this phase.
explain: What can the assistant do through your tool, and what can it not?

nodes.title: Small build: an eval harness with a CI gate
nodes.oneLiner: Build a small harness that runs a fixed set of questions against a model and blocks a change in CI (continuous integration) when the score drops.
nodes.why: Turns 'it feels better' into a number you can gate on.
explain: What makes a score drop real rather than noise?

nodes.title: Retrieval basics (embeddings, pgvector)
nodes.oneLiner: How text becomes vectors and how Postgres with pgvector finds the closest ones.
nodes.why: You built a tiny version in P2; now you understand the database underneath it.
explain: Why does nearest-neighbour search need an index?

nodes.title: Small build: an agent harness
nodes.oneLiner: Wrap your sandbox runner in a thin agent loop with permission modes and a session journal, and use it on your own tasks.
nodes.why: Using an agent you wrote teaches more than reading about harnesses.
explain: What should the journal record so a session can resume?

nodes.title: Small build: a model-swap canary
nodes.oneLiner: Send a small slice of traffic to a new model and promote it only if your eval gate passes.
nodes.why: Ties the AI thread to the capstone: the same gate that protects a fleet protects a model change.
explain: What would make you roll the canary back?

nodes.title: Hash maps, prefix sums, stacks and greedy
nodes.oneLiner: Four building blocks that turn a brute-force scan into one pass: a hash map for lookups, a running prefix sum, a stack for the latest item and a greedy rule.
nodes.why: They are the cheapest speed-ups in a coding round, and almost every later pattern leans on at least one of them.
explain: How does a prefix sum plus a hash map count the subarrays that sum to K?
When is a greedy choice safe?

nodes.title: Sliding window and two pointers
nodes.oneLiner: Move one or two indices through an array or string so each element is visited a constant number of times.
nodes.why: It turns many O(n^2) substring and pair searches into O(n), and it appears constantly in coding rounds.
explain: When does a sliding window work, and what do you do when the window becomes invalid?
Why does 3Sum sort first, and what is its time complexity?

nodes.title: Fast and slow pointers, list reversal, cyclic sort
nodes.oneLiner: Linked-list tricks with two pointer speeds, reversing a list in place, and placing each number at the index equal to its value.
nodes.why: Pointer work without extra memory is a standard coding-round test, and the index-as-value trick finds missing and duplicate numbers in O(1) space.
explain: How does Floyd's cycle detection work, and how do you find where the cycle starts?
How do you reverse a linked list in place?

nodes.title: Intervals, subsets, XOR and modified binary search
nodes.oneLiner: Sort intervals by start and merge or count overlaps, enumerate subsets, use XOR to cancel pairs, and binary search arrays that are only partly sorted.
nodes.why: Four small patterns that each have a standard solution; spotting them quickly saves most of the thinking time in a round.
explain: How do you merge overlapping intervals, and what does it cost?
How do you find the one number that appears once when every other number appears twice?

nodes.title: Design-a-class problems
nodes.oneLiner: Build a small data structure with a clean interface and fixed time bounds, such as an LRU cache, from a blank file.
nodes.why: Lab-style coding rounds often ask for a working class with tests rather than a puzzle, so state, invariants and a clean interface under time pressure matter.
explain: How do you build an LRU cache with O(1) get and put?
How do you get O(1) insert, delete and random element?

nodes.title: Tree DFS, paths and BST properties
nodes.oneLiner: Solve tree problems by deciding what each recursive call returns and what the parent does with it.
nodes.why: Trees are the cleanest place to learn recursion, and the same return-and-combine habit carries into graphs and dynamic programming.
explain: How do you compute the diameter of a binary tree in one pass?
How do you validate a binary search tree?

nodes.title: Tree views, tries, segment trees and Fenwick trees
nodes.oneLiner: Level-order views of a tree, prefix trees for strings, and trees that answer range queries with updates.
nodes.why: Tries and range-query trees appear when a hash map or plain array is too slow for prefix lookups or repeated range queries.
explain: What is a trie, and what does a lookup cost?
When would you use a Fenwick or segment tree instead of a prefix-sum array?

nodes.title: Heaps: top-K, two heaps, K-way merge
nodes.oneLiner: A heap gives the smallest or largest item in O(log n); use it for top-K, running medians and merging sorted lists.
nodes.why: Heaps are the standard tool for best-so-far problems and the engine inside Dijkstra's algorithm and many schedulers.
explain: How do you find the K largest elements of a stream with O(K) memory?
How do two heaps maintain a running median?

nodes.title: Backtracking, monotonic stack, binary search on the answer
nodes.oneLiner: Three patterns built on one invariant each: try-and-undo search, a stack kept in sorted order, and binary search over possible answers.
nodes.why: They look unrelated, but each is solved by stating the invariant first, and they cover many hard-sounding problems with short solutions.
explain: What is a monotonic stack, and what does it find?
When can you binary search on the answer?

nodes.title: Graph traversal: BFS and DFS
nodes.oneLiner: Visit every reachable node with breadth-first or depth-first search on grids and adjacency lists.
nodes.why: Most graph problems reduce to a traversal, so the BFS and DFS templates are the base for everything else in graphs.
explain: When do you pick BFS over DFS?
How do you avoid infinite loops and repeated work in a graph search?

nodes.title: Topological sort
nodes.oneLiner: Order the nodes of a directed graph so every edge points forward, or detect that a cycle makes that impossible.
nodes.why: Dependency problems such as build order, course schedules and task graphs are topological sorts, and so are many scheduling systems.
explain: How does Kahn's algorithm work, and how does it detect a cycle?
How do you topologically sort with DFS?

nodes.title: Union-find
nodes.oneLiner: A structure that tracks which items belong to the same group and merges groups in near-constant time.
nodes.why: It answers connectivity questions on a stream of edges more simply than repeated searches, and it powers Kruskal's minimum spanning tree.
explain: What do path compression and union by rank do?
When is union-find better than DFS for connectivity?

nodes.title: Advanced graphs: shortest paths, spanning trees, bridges
nodes.oneLiner: Weighted shortest paths (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford), minimum spanning trees, bridges and Eulerian paths.
nodes.why: Real systems are weighted graphs, from network routing to cost-aware planning, and these algorithms are the standard answers.
explain: How does Dijkstra's algorithm work, and when does it fail?
How do Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms differ?

nodes.title: Dynamic programming I: 1-D state and subsequences
nodes.oneLiner: Break a problem into overlapping subproblems with one index of state, write the recurrence, and store the results.
nodes.why: DP is the largest family of hard coding-round problems, and the 1-D case teaches the recurrence habit every other DP shape reuses.
explain: How do you choose the state and recurrence for a 1-D DP problem such as House Robber?
What is the difference between memoisation and tabulation?

nodes.title: Dynamic programming II: 2-D grids and two-string DP
nodes.oneLiner: DP over a grid or over two strings, where the state is a pair of indices and each cell depends on its neighbours.
nodes.why: Edit distance, longest common subsequence and path counting are the classic two-index tables, and they appear in diff tools and sequence alignment.
explain: State the recurrence for longest common subsequence.
State the recurrence for edit distance.

nodes.title: Dynamic programming III: knapsack, palindromes, stock and game
nodes.oneLiner: Knapsack-style choices under a capacity, palindrome substrings, buy-and-sell stock states and two-player game DP.
nodes.why: Knapsack and its variants model resource allocation under a budget, which is the shape of many real scheduling and packing questions.
explain: How do 0/1 knapsack and unbounded knapsack differ in the DP?
How do you model the stock problem with a cooldown as DP?

nodes.title: Dynamic programming IV: intervals, bitmask, state machines
nodes.oneLiner: DP over intervals, over bitmasks of chosen items, and over small state machines: the hardest DP problems.
nodes.why: These are the high-difficulty DP shapes, and knowing the template for each lets you recognise them instead of searching blind.
explain: What is the interval DP template, using Burst Balloons?
When is bitmask DP applicable, and what does it cost?

nodes.title: The design method
nodes.oneLiner: A fixed order for a design round: requirements, numbers, API and data model, boxes, a deep dive, then failure modes.
nodes.why: A repeatable method keeps you from wandering and shows your reasoning at each step, and every other design node plugs into it.
explain: What are the steps of a design round, in order?
Why define the API and data model before drawing boxes?

nodes.title: Estimation and capacity numbers
nodes.oneLiner: Rough numbers for latency, throughput, storage and cost, good enough to choose a design.
nodes.why: A design is only sensible at a given scale, and five minutes of arithmetic tells you whether one machine, a cache or a sharded cluster is needed.
explain: A service gets 100 million requests per day. What are the average and peak request rates?
Roughly how much storage do 1 billion records of 1 KB need, with 3 replicas?

nodes.title: Relational storage and transactions
nodes.oneLiner: Tables, joins and ACID transactions: what a relational database guarantees and when it stops being enough.
nodes.why: Most systems start on a relational database, and knowing what transactions and isolation levels protect tells you when you can stay on one.
explain: What do the ACID properties mean?
How would you stop two users booking the same seat?

nodes.title: Indexing
nodes.oneLiner: Data structures that make lookups fast: B-trees, hash indexes, LSM trees and geospatial indexes.
nodes.why: An index is the difference between scanning a table and reaching one row, and every query-heavy design depends on choosing the right one.
explain: Why does a B-tree index speed up a query, and what does it cost?
How would you find nearby drivers or restaurants?

nodes.title: Replication
nodes.oneLiner: Keeping copies of data on several machines: leader-follower, multi-leader and leaderless setups, and the lag between copies.
nodes.why: Replication is how a system survives machine loss and serves more reads, and it is the source of most consistency questions.
explain: What is replication lag, and how does it show up for users?
How do synchronous and asynchronous replication differ?

nodes.title: Partitioning
nodes.oneLiner: Splitting data across machines by key range or hash so that no single machine holds or serves it all.
nodes.why: Partitioning is what lets storage and traffic grow beyond one machine, and hot keys and rebalancing are where designs go wrong.
explain: Compare range partitioning with hash partitioning.
Why use consistent hashing?

nodes.title: NoSQL and key-value stores
nodes.oneLiner: Key-value, document and wide-column stores that trade joins and strong transactions for scale and availability.
nodes.why: Dynamo-style stores are the standard answer when data is huge, access is by key, and the system must stay available through failures.
explain: How does a Dynamo-style store use quorums for reads and writes?
When would you choose an LSM-tree-based store?

nodes.title: Object storage and file systems
nodes.oneLiner: Storing large blobs and files durably: metadata kept apart from data, chunking, and replication or erasure coding.
nodes.why: Object storage underlies backups, media and data lakes, and the split between metadata and data shows up in nearly every file system design.
explain: How is an object store like S3 designed at a high level?
Why use erasure coding instead of three copies?

nodes.title: Consensus and coordination
nodes.oneLiner: Getting several machines to agree on one value or one leader: Raft and Paxos, leases, locks and ordering.
nodes.why: Leader election, locks and metadata stores all need agreement that survives failures, and etcd and ZooKeeper package it.
explain: What does Raft guarantee, and how many failures does it tolerate?
Why is a distributed lock with only a timeout unsafe, and what fixes it?

nodes.title: Caching
nodes.oneLiner: Keeping hot data in fast memory in front of a slower store: cache-aside, write-through, eviction and invalidation.
nodes.why: Caching is the first fix for read-heavy load and latency, and getting invalidation and stampedes right is the real design work.
explain: Compare cache-aside, write-through and write-back.
What is a cache stampede, and how do you prevent it?

nodes.title: CDN, load balancing and gateways
nodes.oneLiner: Spreading traffic across servers and pushing static and media content close to users.
nodes.why: These layers sit in front of every large system and decide availability, latency and where the traffic limits are.
explain: What does a CDN do, and what can it not do well?
How do layer-4 and layer-7 load balancers differ?

nodes.title: Rate limiting
nodes.oneLiner: Capping how many requests a client can make in a time window, in one process or across a fleet.
nodes.why: Rate limits protect shared systems from overload and abuse, and the distributed version is a standard design question about counters and races.
explain: Explain the token bucket algorithm.
How do you enforce one limit across many servers?

nodes.title: Queues and streams
nodes.oneLiner: Decoupling producers from consumers with queues and logs: delivery guarantees, ordering, partitions and replay.
nodes.why: Queues absorb bursts and let parts of a system fail independently, and streams add replay and are the base of pipelines and analytics.
explain: How do a message queue and a log-based stream such as Kafka differ?
What does exactly-once delivery mean in practice?

nodes.title: Search and retrieval
nodes.oneLiner: Finding documents by words or by meaning: inverted indexes, ranking, typeahead, and vector search for retrieval-augmented generation.
nodes.why: Search and retrieval recur everywhere, from product search to feeding relevant context to a language model.
explain: What is an inverted index?
How does vector search work for RAG, and what is its main trade-off?

nodes.title: Feeds and fan-out
nodes.oneLiner: Building each user's timeline: fan-out on write, fan-out on read, and a hybrid for accounts with huge followings.
nodes.why: The feed is the classic read-heavy design and the clearest case of precomputing versus computing on demand.
explain: Compare fan-out on write with fan-out on read.
How do real feed systems handle celebrity accounts?

nodes.title: Notifications and real-time messaging
nodes.oneLiner: Delivering events to people: push, email and in-app notifications, and persistent connections for chat and live updates.
nodes.why: Delivery to people is unreliable and rate-limited, so these designs are about retries, preferences, fan-out and connection management.
explain: How would you make a notification system reliable?
How does a chat server deliver a message to a recipient?

nodes.title: Payments and idempotency
nodes.oneLiner: Moving money safely: idempotency keys, a ledger, retries without double charges, and reconciliation.
nodes.why: Payments show why retries need idempotency and why a correct ledger matters more than speed.
explain: What is an idempotency key, and how does it prevent double charges?
Why use an append-only ledger and reconciliation?

nodes.title: LLM gateway
nodes.oneLiner: A single front door for model calls: routing, caching, rate limits, cost tracking, fallbacks and safe rollout of prompts and models.
nodes.why: Every team calling models needs the same controls, and a gateway puts cost, reliability and policy in one place.
explain: What does an LLM gateway do for a company?
What can an LLM gateway cache, and what are the risks?

nodes.title: Inference platform
nodes.oneLiner: Serving models at scale: batching, the KV cache, GPU scheduling, autoscaling and latency targets.
nodes.why: Inference is most of the running cost of an AI product, so batching and memory use decide both latency and price.
explain: Why does continuous batching improve GPU utilisation?
What is the KV cache, and why does it limit concurrency?

nodes.title: Training platform
nodes.oneLiner: Running large training jobs across many GPUs: data and model parallelism, checkpoints, scheduling and failure recovery.
nodes.why: At large scale hardware fails during every long run, so checkpointing and scheduling decide whether a run finishes.
explain: Why do large training runs checkpoint, and how often?
What do data parallelism and tensor or pipeline parallelism each split?

nodes.title: Evaluation pipeline
nodes.oneLiner: Measuring whether a new model or prompt is better: datasets, automated graders, human review and release gates.
nodes.why: Without a trustworthy measure you cannot ship model changes safely, and the evaluation pipeline is the gate.
explain: What are the parts of an evaluation pipeline for a model release?
What are the risks of using an LLM as a judge?

nodes.title: Agent platforms
nodes.oneLiner: Running agents safely at scale: orchestration loops, memory, sandboxed code execution, permissions and observability.
nodes.why: An agent is a model in a loop with tools, so the platform must bound what it can do, remember context and make every run traceable.
explain: Why run agent-written code in a sandbox, and how?
How do you make an agent run observable and recoverable?

tickets.title: Watch 3Blue1Brown neural networks, chapters 1 to 3
tickets.text:
Watch the three videos in order, about 52 minutes. Skip chapter 4, which is the calculus.
Take away: a network is one big function with adjustable weights. Training is repeated small steps that lower a loss. Backpropagation is the bookkeeping for those steps, which is why training needs far more memory than serving.
Done when you can say what a weight is and what one step of gradient descent does.

links.label: 3Blue1Brown: But what is a neural network? (18:40)
3Blue1Brown: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn (20:33)

explain: What is a weight, and why does a bigger model need more memory?
explainAnswers: A weight is one adjustable number inside the network; training nudges millions or billions of them until the output is right. Every weight has to be stored, so a model with more weights needs more memory just to hold them. For example, 70 billion weights at 2 bytes each is about 140 GB.

tickets.title: Run a small model on your laptop
tickets.text:
Run one small model on your own laptop and measure it.
Before you start: open Activity Monitor and check free memory. A 3-billion-parameter model at 4-bit needs about 2 to 3 GB. If memory is tight, pick the 1-billion model, close heavy apps, and stop if the laptop slows down.
Do: (1) install Ollama and run `ollama run llama3.2:3b --verbose`; (2) send a one-line prompt and write down the "eval rate" it prints, in tokens per second; (3) paste in a prompt of about 2,000 words and note the "prompt eval rate"; (4) watch memory while it answers.
Take away: reading a prompt is much faster per token than writing the answer.
Done when you can say both rates and what limited the slower one.

tickets.title: Watch 3Blue1Brown on transformers and attention
tickets.text:
Watch both videos in order, about 53 minutes.
Take away: text becomes tokens, tokens become vectors, attention mixes information between positions, and the model outputs a probability for every possible next token. Attention compares every pair of positions, so long context is expensive, and masking is why past keys and values can be cached.
Done when you can say why a longer prompt costs more.
explain: What does attention look at when the model picks the next token?
Why does a longer prompt cost more?
explainAnswers: It looks back at the earlier tokens in the prompt and scores how relevant each one is to the token being produced. The highest-scoring tokens contribute most to the next prediction. It never looks ahead, because those tokens do not exist yet.

Attention compares every token with every earlier token, so the work grows faster than the prompt length. The model also has to keep keys and values for every token in memory (the KV cache). More tokens means more compute to read the prompt and more memory held while answering.

tickets.title: Set up vLLM on a free GPU
tickets.text:
Use a free Modal or Kaggle GPU. No card should be charged: if Modal asks for a card, use Kaggle instead.
Install vLLM, start its server with an instruct model of 1 to 3 billion parameters and send one request with curl. Stop the session when you are done so no quota is spent.
Check: a completion comes back and the server log shows the model loaded.
Done when you can repeat the setup from your notes.

tickets.title: Measure vLLM on the free GPU
tickets.text:
Start the server again and send 20 requests with a small script. Open the `/metrics` page and write down the KV-cache use and the tokens per second. `/metrics` holds cumulative counters, so your script must read it twice and divide the change in generated tokens by the seconds between the readings. Compare the result with your laptop numbers from the earlier ticket. Stop the session when you are done so no quota is spent.
With only 20 requests on a small model the KV cache will be barely used, so "nothing limited it yet" is an honest answer for the cache. Then say what the GPU did limit, for example the memory bandwidth needed to read the weights for each generated token.
Done when you can say what limited throughput on the GPU.
explain: How many tokens per second did you get, and what limited it?
explainAnswers: On your laptop a small model typically writes a few tens of tokens per second. On the free GPU, 20 requests batched together reach a much higher total, typically hundreds of tokens per second. In both cases each decode step is limited by how fast the weights are read from memory, and batching shares that one read across all the requests.

tickets.title: Watch Karpathy's Deep Dive into LLMs, part 1
tickets.text:
Watch from 0:00:00 to 0:31:09, about 31 minutes: where the data comes from, tokenisation (at 07:47), how the network reads tokens and writes a probability for the next one (at 14:27), and what inference is.
Take away: text is cut into tokens, and tokens, not characters, are what a model sees, what you are billed for and what limits the context.
Done when you can say what a token is and why a model sees tokens rather than characters.

links.label: Andrej Karpathy: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT (3:31:23)

tickets.title: Watch Karpathy's Deep Dive into LLMs, part 2
tickets.text:
Watch from 0:31:09 to 1:20:32, about 49 minutes: training and running GPT-2, running a Llama 3.1 base model, the step from pretraining to post-training, and how conversation data teaches the model to be an assistant.
Take away: a base model is an autocomplete of internet text; post-training is what turns it into an assistant.
Done when you can say what a base model is and why it is not an assistant yet.

links.label: Andrej Karpathy: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT (3:31:23)

tickets.title: Read the structured-output documentation
tickets.text:
Read the tool-use overview (about 15 minutes) and the structured outputs page (about 15 minutes).
Take away: a model can be asked for JSON that matches a schema, and your code still has to check the answer.
Done when you can list two ways an answer can be almost valid.

tickets.title: Write the schema and the validator for a structured-output client
tickets.text:
Build `llmjson.py`, the first half of a structured-output client. Use any hosted model API; the tests must not call it.
1. Define a schema for a triage result: category (bug, question or feature), urgency from 1 to 5, a one-sentence summary.
2. Write `validate(text)`: parse the JSON, check the keys, types and ranges, and return the object or raise `ValidationError` with a message that says what is wrong.
3. Write `ask(prompt, call)`, where `call` returns the model's text: call once, validate, return the object.
4. Test `validate` with five bad replies (not JSON, a missing key, a wrong type, urgency 9, text around the JSON) and one good one.
Done when `python -m pytest` passes. The next ticket adds retries.

tickets.title: Watch Karpathy's Deep Dive into LLMs, part 3: tools and memory
tickets.text:
Watch from 1:20:32 to 1:41:46, about 21 minutes: hallucinations, tool use, and knowledge in the weights versus working memory in the context.
Take away: tool use is special tokens that your own code intercepts, and the context window is the model's working memory.
Done when you can say how a tool call gets from the model to your code.

links.label: Andrej Karpathy: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT (3:31:23)

tickets.title: Try Tiktokenizer, then read how models sample text
tickets.text:
Part 1, 20 minutes: open Tiktokenizer, pick a modern model's tokenizer and paste in (a) an English paragraph, (b) a Go source file, (c) deeply nested JSON, (d) a long number, (e) non-English text, (f) the same word with and without a leading space. Note how tokens per character varies.
Part 2, 15 minutes: read the Hugging Face post on greedy search, beam search, temperature, top-k and top-p. Read for the ideas; the code samples are old.
Done when you can say what a higher temperature and a lower top-p each change about the next-token choice.

links.label: Hugging Face: How to generate text

tickets.title: Add retries with backoff and tests
tickets.text:
Change `ask` in `llmjson.py` to `ask(prompt, call, sleep=time.sleep)` and make it retry when `validate` raises `ValidationError`: up to 3 retries, so at most 4 calls in all. Nothing else is retried: an error raised by `call` itself (a network failure, say) goes straight up.
Each retry sends the original prompt plus the error message (`str(error)`) of the reply that just failed; do not pile up older errors. Before each retry call `sleep(delay)`: 0.1 s the first time, 0.2 the second, 0.4 the third. There is no sleep after the last failure, and the 4th failed reply raises its `ValidationError` out of `ask`.
Tests (a fake `call` that records the prompts it gets, and a `sleep` that records instead of waiting):
1. The fake returns `oops`, then `still not json`, then a good reply. Assert `ask` returns the good object, there were exactly 3 calls, the sleeps were [0.1, 0.2] (compare with `pytest.approx`), the first prompt is your original prompt, and the second prompt contains your original prompt and the message that `validate("oops")` raises.
2. The fake returns `oops` every time. Assert `ask` raises `ValidationError` after exactly 4 calls, with sleeps [0.1, 0.2, 0.4].
3. The fake returns a good reply first. Assert 1 call and no sleeps.
Done when `python -m pytest` passes.

tickets.title: Watch Karpathy's Deep Dive into LLMs, part 4: reinforcement learning
tickets.text:
Watch two segments of the same video, about 41 minutes: 2:07:28 to 2:27:47 (from supervised fine-tuning to reinforcement learning) and 2:48:26 to 3:09:39 (RLHF). Skip the rest.
Take away: reasoning models write long chains of thought, which means many output tokens and a lot of decode time on your GPUs.
Done when you can say why a reasoning model costs more to serve.

links.label: Andrej Karpathy: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT (3:31:23)

explain: Why does a reasoning model cost more to serve than a chat model for the same question?
What does RLHF add after supervised fine-tuning, and why does an infra engineer care?
explainAnswers: A reasoning model writes a long chain of thought before it answers, so it produces many more output tokens. Decode makes one token at a time and every step re-reads the weights from memory, so it is limited by memory bandwidth and the GPU-seconds grow with the number of tokens. The request also holds its KV cache for the whole, longer generation, which leaves less room to batch other users. The user sees one answer, but the cluster pays for thousands of hidden tokens.

RLHF first trains a separate reward model on human preference ratings, then tunes the language model to earn higher scores from it. That training loop has to generate many sampled answers and score each one, which is inference work inside training. So it needs more training compute than supervised fine-tuning on fixed examples, plus rollout and serving infrastructure running beside the trainer.

tickets.title: Read about RAG, agents, tool use and MCP
tickets.text:
Four short readings, about 57 minutes in all: contextual retrieval (about 12), building effective agents (about 20), the tool-use overview (about 15) and the MCP introduction (about 10).
Take away: RAG is retrieval pasted into a prompt; an agent is a model in a loop that calls tools; MCP is a standard way to plug tools in.
Done when you can draw the tool-use loop in four boxes.

tickets.title: Read the Claude Code best-practice guide
tickets.text:
Skim the Claude Code overview, then read the Best practices page. It covers how to give an agent context (a CLAUDE.md), how to ask for a plan before code (plan mode) and how to check its work.
Take away: an agent does what the instructions say, so write down how to run the tests and what must not be touched.
Done when you have a list of three things to put in your own CLAUDE.md.

tickets.title: Set up a delegation log and hand three real tasks to an agent
tickets.text:
Pick a repo you work in. Add a short CLAUDE.md: what the repo is, how to run its tests, what the agent must not touch. Create `delegation-log.md` with the columns date, task, what I asked, what came back, what I redid and why.
Hand three real tasks to Claude Code this week and fill one row for each. Pick tasks you can check: a small refactor, a test you were putting off, an explanation of code you do not know. Do not paste anything you are not allowed to share.
Done when the log has three rows and you can say which task you would not delegate again.
explain: Which task did you delegate this week that you would not delegate again, and why?
explainAnswers: There is no single right answer; it is your own log. A good answer names a task where the agent's output looked right but needed a lot of rework, or where a mistake would have been costly. It then says what would have to change, such as a clearer request or a check you can run, before you would delegate it again.

tickets.title: Add a repair path for almost-valid JSON
tickets.text:
In `llmjson.py` add `repair(text)` and use it in `ask` before spending a retry: when `validate` rejects a reply, run `validate(repair(reply))`; if that passes, return the object without another call and without a sleep. `validate` itself stays strict. `repair` does three things, in this order: (1) if the text starts with a code-fence line (three backticks, with or without a word such as json after them), drop that line and the closing fence line of three backticks; (2) keep only the text from the first `{` to the last `}` (leave it alone if there is no pair); (3) remove a comma that sits right before a `}` or `]`, with `re.sub(r",\s*([}\]])", r"\1", text)`.
Add these five malformed replies to the tests, each wrapping or breaking this object: `{"category": "bug", "urgency": 3, "summary": "Login fails."}`
1. The object inside a code fence: a line of three backticks followed by json, the object, then a line of three backticks.
2. The same fence with no json after the opening backticks.
3. The object with a comma after the last value: `..."Login fails.",}`.
4. The text `Here is the result: ` before the object.
5. Fence, trailing comma and text around it, all at once: the line `Sure, here you go:`, then the fenced object from 1 with the trailing comma from 3, then the line `Let me know if you need more.`.
Check: for each of the five, `ask` returns the object after exactly 1 call and no sleep. Then add two more tests: a reply of `I cannot help with that.` followed by a good reply gives 2 calls and sleeps [0.1]; a fenced reply whose urgency is 9 followed by a good reply also gives 2 calls (repair cannot fix a bad value). The tests from the previous ticket must still pass.
Done when `python -m pytest` passes.
explain: What do you do when the model returns almost-valid JSON?
explainAnswers: First try a cheap repair, such as stripping a code fence or a trailing comma, and validate again. If it still fails, retry with the validation error in the prompt so the model can correct itself. Stop after a small number of tries and raise an error rather than looping.

tickets.title: Read Transformer Math 101 and the first chapters of Inference Engineering
tickets.text:
Read the EleutherAI post (12 minutes) for bytes per parameter and the 6 x parameters x tokens rule. Then read Baseten's Inference Engineering chapter 0, section 1.4 (TTFT, inter-token latency, goodput) and chapter 2 sections 2.1, 2.2, 2.4 and 2.5 (about 31 minutes). Skip 2.3.
Take away: prefill is compute-bound and sets time to first token; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and sets inter-token latency; the KV cache grows with context times concurrent sequences.
Done when you can say which of prefill and decode a long prompt stresses.

tickets.title: Read the tokensim brief and a simulation primer
tickets.text:
The brief: tokensim is a simulated LLM engine, a load generator and a fake OpenAI-style server, and its `make check` must pass on every step. Then read the SimPy tutorial (25 minutes) or, if you prefer to write the loop by hand, the description of a discrete-event simulation.
Take away: a clock and a queue of timed events is the whole idea.
Done when you can sketch the event loop.

tickets.title: Lay out the tokensim lab: Makefile targets and a results file
tickets.text:
Create `labs/b1-tokensim` with a Makefile whose targets are `up`, `run`, `check` and `down` (the first and last may do nothing yet), and a tiny reporter that writes `results.json`: `{ "checks": [{ "id", "name", "status", "detail", "metrics" }], "summary": { "pass", "fail", "skip" } }`, where status is pass, fail or skip.
Check: `make check` writes a file with one passing check named `layout`.
Done when it does.

tickets.title: Read kipply on inference arithmetic and the PagedAttention story
tickets.text:
Read kipply's post (30 minutes): the KV cache, capacity and latency sections, and skim parallelism. The numbers are A100-era and assume full multi-head attention, so read for the method; the memory worksheet redoes them for a modern model. Then read the vLLM post (10 minutes) on why naive KV allocation wastes memory and how paging fixes it.
Done when you can say why paging the KV cache raises throughput.

links.label: vLLM: Easy, Fast, and Cheap LLM Serving with PagedAttention

tickets.title: Work the GPU memory sums as a small script
tickets.text:
Write memsum.py, a script that takes a model's config.json values and prints weight bytes and KV-cache bytes per token. Weights = parameters x bytes per parameter (bf16 2, fp8 1, int4 0.5). KV bytes per token = 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes per element. Use grouped-query attention's kv_heads, not the attention head count.
Check values: Llama 3.1 70B in bf16 is 327,680 bytes per token (80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128); Llama 3.1 8B is 131,072.
Then answer on paper: (1) how many 80 GB GPUs for 70B bf16 at 32k context and 16 users, (2) the same with fp8 and int4, (3) whether weights or KV hit first, (4) what 8 KV heads instead of 64 buys, (5) whether prefill of 8k tokens or decode of 500 tokens dominates the total response time, and which one sets time to first token.
Done when memsum.py reproduces both check values and you can answer all five.

tickets.title: Work the training compute sum
tickets.text:
Add train_compute.py beside memsum.py. Compute C = 6 x parameters x tokens for Llama 3.1 70B on about 15 trillion tokens (treat the token count as approximate), divide by an effective 4e14 FLOP/s per H100 (about 40% of the bf16 peak) and print GPU-hours.
Check value: about 6.3e24 FLOPs and about 4.4 million H100-hours.
Take away: this is why pretraining is for a dozen organisations and why you will host and fine-tune, not pretrain.
Done when the script prints both numbers and you can say what utilisation does to the answer.

tickets.title: Read about GPU hardware, inference engines and the first optimisation levers
tickets.text:
Read Inference Engineering section 3.1 (GPU architecture), 4.3 (inference engines) and chapter 5 sections 5.1, 5.3, 5.4 and 5.5 (quantisation, caching, model parallelism, disaggregation), about 36 minutes in all.
Take away: prefix caching and tensor parallelism are the first levers; FP8 is the default on recent GPUs.
Done when you can say what prefix caching saves and when it does not help.

tickets.title: Read about the roofline: when a GPU waits for memory
tickets.text:
Read the "All about rooflines" chapter (about 30 minutes) and the roofline entry in the Modal GPU glossary (about 10 minutes).
Take away: a piece of work is compute-bound or memory-bound depending on how many operations it does per byte it reads, compared with the GPU's ratio of compute to memory bandwidth. Decoding one token reads every weight once for about two operations each, so it sits far on the memory side. Reading a long prompt reuses each weight across many tokens, so it sits on the compute side.
Done when you can work out the ridge point of a GPU from its two datasheet numbers.

links.label: How to Scale Your Model, rooflines

tickets.title: Write the roofline function and test decode
tickets.text:
Write `roofline.py` with a function `step_time(flops, bytes_read, peak_flops, bandwidth)` that returns the larger of flops / peak_flops and bytes_read / bandwidth, and says which one limits. Use round numbers for one H100: 1e15 FLOP/s (bf16) and 3.35e12 bytes/s; check the datasheet before you quote them anywhere. Model decode: one token reads all the weights once and does 2 x parameters operations.
Check value: a 70B-parameter model in fp8 (70e9 bytes) decodes one token in about 20.9 ms (about 48 tokens a second) and is memory-bound. Test it within 2%.
Keep the function importable: tokensim uses it in a later step. The next ticket adds prefill.
Done when `python -m pytest` passes with that number.

tickets.title: Add prefill and a ridge-point report
tickets.text:
In `roofline.py` add prefill: n prompt tokens do 2 x parameters x n operations on one read of the weights. Add `ridge_point(peak_flops, bandwidth)`, the operations per byte at which the two limits meet, and print it for the H100 numbers.
Check values: prefilling 8,000 tokens of the 70B fp8 model takes about 1.12 s (2 x 70e9 x 8,000 / 1e15) and is compute-bound; the ridge point is about 299 operations per byte (1e15 / 3.35e12). Test both within 2%.
Done when `python -m pytest` passes.
explain: Why is decode memory-bound while prefill is compute-bound?
What does a roofline chart tell you that a profiler does not?
explainAnswers: In decode each step reads all the weights to produce just one token, so there are few calculations per byte read and memory is the limit. In prefill the same weights are reused across thousands of prompt tokens, so there are many calculations per byte and the compute units are the limit. The ratio of calculations to bytes read decides which side you are on.

A roofline shows the best speed the hardware could reach for work of a given intensity, so you can see how close you are and which limit applies. A profiler shows where time went but not what the ceiling is. Together they tell you whether to optimise the code or accept the hardware limit.

tickets.title: Read about quantisation
tickets.text:
Skim the visual guide to quantisation (30 minutes; there are many figures) and read the abstract of the BF16 paper (5 minutes). Do the GPU memory worksheet before this ticket so the numbers have somewhere to land.
Take away: INT4 weight-only fits a model on fewer GPUs, and FP8 is close to lossless on recent hardware; you must still re-evaluate a quantised model.
Done when you can name what you give up with 4-bit weights.

links.label: Maarten Grootendorst: A Visual Guide to Quantization
Give Me BF16 or Give Me Death? (abstract)

tickets.title: Write the event loop and the request records
tickets.text:
In the tokensim lab, write `engine.py`: the event loop of a discrete-event simulator. A request has an arrival time, a prompt length and an output length. The engine has a clock and a priority queue of timed events; write it by hand or with SimPy. For now every step takes a fixed time you pass in (the roofline times come in the next ticket) and the engine serves one request at a time. Emit one record per request: arrival, time to first token, finish time, tokens.
Check (add to `make check`): with a prefill time of 1.0 s and 0.02 s per decode step, a request with 500 output tokens (the first comes from the prefill, then 499 decode steps) has time to first token 1.0 s and finish time 10.98 s.
Done when `make check` passes.

tickets.title: Use roofline step times and check one request
tickets.text:
Make the roofline times the default: a prefill step takes the roofline time for the prompt, and a decode step the roofline time to read the weights once (use the function from the T01 tickets; the KV reads come in the next ticket). Keep the fixed-time option, so the check from the previous ticket still passes.
Check (add to `make check`): for one request of 8,000 prompt tokens and 500 output tokens on the 70B fp8 example, time to first token is within 1% of the prefill time from your calculator (1.12 s), and total time is within 3% of prefill plus 499 decode steps of 20.9 ms (about 11.55 s). The 3% leaves room for the KV reads that the next tickets add, which cost about 2% on this request.
Done when `make check` passes and prints the time to first token and the time per token.

tickets.title: Read about autoscaling and the metrics a serving engine exposes
tickets.text:
Read Inference Engineering section 7.2 on autoscaling (10 minutes). Read the vLLM production metrics page (20 minutes) and map each metric to an alert or an autoscaling idea; do not start a server.
Done when you can say what you would look at first if time to first token went up.

tickets.title: Read how to benchmark an LLM endpoint fairly
tickets.text:
Read the AIPerf article (about 25 minutes): arrival patterns, streaming so you can see time to first token and inter-token latency, and percentiles. Then read the vLLM metrics design page (about 15 minutes): which metric answers which question.
Take away: a fair benchmark fixes the load, warms up first, repeats the run, reports an error bar, and judges goodput (requests that meet both latency targets) rather than raw throughput.
Done when you can list what a fair benchmark fixes.

links.label: NVIDIA, Benchmarking LLM inference at scale with AIPerf

tickets.title: Write a fake endpoint and a fixed-load client
tickets.text:
Write `fake_endpoint.py` (about 30 lines, standard library only). Use `ThreadingHTTPServer` so every request is served on its own thread: a single-threaded server would queue requests (each one holds it for about 210 ms against a 200 ms gap between requests) and the median would drift far above 110 ms. It streams a reply: the first token after 100 ms plus a random jitter drawn uniformly from 0 to 20 ms, then 10 more tokens 10 ms apart.
Write `bench.py`: send requests at a fixed 5 per second for 20 seconds and print each request's time to first token.
Check: the median is between 105 and 115 ms (100 ms plus jitter of 0 to 20 ms, which averages 10 ms, should put it near 110).
Done when the check passes.

tickets.title: Add warm-up, repeats and an error bar
tickets.text:
In `bench.py` drop the first 10 seconds of each run as warm-up, repeat the whole run 5 times (make the repeat count an option), and print the median time to first token of each repeat, the mean of those medians and a 95% t-interval on that mean (mean plus or minus t x s / sqrt(repeats), where s is the sample standard deviation of the medians, dividing by n-1, and t = 4.30 for 3 repeats, 2.78 for 5 and 2.262 for 10).
Check the interval code on known numbers: for the three values 1, 2, 3 the half-width is 2.48, and for the ten values 1 to 10 it is 2.17 (test both within 0.01). Do not compare two real runs for a narrower interval: with only 3 repeats the spread is itself so uncertain that a correct tool often shows no clear difference.
Done when both known-number checks pass.
explain: How do you benchmark an LLM endpoint fairly?
What is goodput and why does it beat throughput?
explainAnswers: Fix the load (arrival rate, prompt and output lengths), warm the system up and throw those results away, then repeat the run several times. Report a median with an error bar, not a single number, and record the model, version and hardware. Measure time to first token and inter-token latency separately.

Goodput counts only the requests that met their latency targets, while throughput counts everything served. A system can show high throughput while most users wait too long. Goodput measures what users actually find acceptable, so it is the number to optimise.

tickets.title: Read about evals, leaderboards and scaling laws
tickets.text:
Read Anthropic's post on evals (20 minutes). Look at LMArena and the lm-evaluation-harness readme (15 minutes) to see what a leaderboard is. Read the Chinchilla abstract (5 minutes).
Take away: an eval is an input plus a grader, a leaderboard is one kind of eval, and compute is roughly 6 x parameters x tokens.
Done when you can say why a quantised deployment must be re-evaluated.

links.label: Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents

explain: Why is decode slow even on a fast GPU?
What is the KV cache (key-value cache) saving?
explainAnswers: Decode produces one token at a time, and each step must read every weight from memory. The GPU spends its time waiting for memory, not calculating, so memory bandwidth sets the speed. A faster calculator does not help much; more bandwidth or batching does.

It stores the keys and values already computed for earlier tokens so the model does not recompute them at every step. Without it, each new token would redo the work for the whole prompt. The price is memory, which grows with context length and with the number of users served at once.

tickets.title: Add continuous batching
tickets.text:
Let the engine run many requests at once: each step decodes one token for every running request, a waiting request is prefilled as soon as it arrives (the decode steps pause while it is), and a finished request leaves at once. Step time is the roofline time for reading the weights once plus the KV reads: the tokens held by the running requests x 163,840 bytes per token divided by the bandwidth. That number is the KV bytes per token of this model with 1-byte (fp8) elements: run your memsum script with 1 byte per KV element. Do not copy the 327,680 from the memory-sums ticket, which is the bf16 value; with it the totals in the roofline ticket and the batch sizes below would be wrong.
Check: send 16 identical requests, each 1,000 prompt tokens and 500 output tokens, all arriving at time 0. Throughput (16 x 500 output tokens divided by the time the last one finishes) is at least 8 times the throughput of one such request alone (about 47 tokens a second alone, so expect roughly 600 with batching), and never above 16 x 3.35e12 / 70e9 = 766 tokens a second, the most the memory could feed.
Done when the check passes.

tickets.title: Add the KV memory limit
tickets.text:
A request is held back when its KV cache would not fit. When a request starts, reserve KV space for the whole request (prompt plus output tokens x 163,840 bytes per token, the fp8 value from memsum with 1-byte KV elements, not the bf16 327,680) out of a budget in bytes that you pass in, and give the space back when it finishes. A budget smaller than one request can never finish it: refuse that budget with a clear error.
Check: with a budget that holds exactly 4 of the 1,000 + 500 token requests, never more than 4 run at once and all 16 still finish; with a budget of 100 GB the throughput is within 1% of the previous step's.
Done when the check passes.

tickets.title: Read about tail latency and Little's law
tickets.text:
Read The Tail at Scale (about 25 minutes), then the Little's law page (about 10 minutes).
Take away: when one request fans out to many servers, the slowest 1% dominates. If a request waits for 100 servers and each is slow 1% of the time, 63% of requests meet at least one slow server (1 - 0.99^100). Little's law: the average number of items in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends there.
Done when you can say why the slowest 1% dominates when a request fans out to many servers, and what Little's law says.

tickets.title: Simulate a single queue and compare p99 with the formula
tickets.text:
Write `queue_sim.py`: one server, random arrivals and service times (an M/M/1 queue), 200,000 jobs. Take service rate mu = 1 job per second, so arrival rate lambda = utilisation rho. For utilisation 0.5, 0.7, 0.85 and 0.95 print the mean wait in the queue and the p99 wait next to the formula mean wait = rho / (mu - lambda).
Check values: the formula gives 1.0, 2.33, 5.67 and 19.0 seconds. The simulated mean should be within 5% at 0.5, within 7% at 0.7, within 15% at 0.85 and within 40% at 0.95. The 0.95 value is noisy: the queue is long and slow to settle, so one run can be well off, and that noise is itself a sign of the knee (you may drop the first 10% of jobs as warm-up). Little's law, L = lambda x W with L the time-average number of jobs in the system and W the mean time in the system, should hold within 2% at every utilisation.
