Save the table: the write-up uses it.
Done when the table prints and both checks pass.

tickets.title: Write the open-loop and closed-loop load generators
tickets.text:
Open loop: requests arrive at a fixed average rate whatever the engine does (Poisson arrivals: the gaps are drawn from an exponential distribution with mean 1 / rate). Closed loop: a fixed number of users, each sends the next request when the last one finishes. Prompt and output lengths come from two distributions you choose (say so in the README); keep every length between a third and three times its median, so one huge request cannot swamp a run.
Check: for the open-loop generator at 50 requests a second over 200 simulated seconds (10,000 expected arrivals, no engine needed) the arrival count is within 5% of rate x time. That is five standard deviations of the count, so a correct generator passes every time (3% would fail now and then). With the engine attached, the closed-loop generator never has more than the user count in flight.
Done when both checks pass.

tickets.title: Write one page on why p99 explodes near 85% utilisation
tickets.text:
Write one page (about 350 words) for a teammate whose service runs at 85% utilisation and whose p99 keeps getting worse. Use your own numbers from the queue simulation: a small table of utilisation against mean and p99 wait, and one sentence that points at the knee. Say what Little's law tells you, what you would change first (capacity, batching or admission control) and what you would measure to know it worked.
It is graded against the design rubric: requirements and numbers, trade-offs, and what a stronger version would do.
explain: Why does p99 explode near 85% utilisation?
What does Little's law say, in one sentence?
explainAnswers: As a server gets close to full, any burst of arrivals forms a queue that takes a long time to drain. Waiting time grows steeply (roughly as one divided by the capacity left over): at 85% utilisation the queueing wait is already about 5.7 times the service time (utilisation divided by one minus utilisation), and it grows steeply after that, so small increases in load cause big increases in delay. The slowest 1% of requests, which meet the longest queues, get far worse than the average.

The average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each item spends there. If requests arrive at 10 per second and each takes 2 seconds in the system, about 20 are in flight on average. It holds for any stable system, whatever the details.

tickets.title: Read the USE method for finding a bottleneck
tickets.text:
Read Brendan Gregg's USE Method page (about 20 minutes), then the py-spy readme (about 10 minutes).
Take away: for every resource, ask for its utilisation, saturation and errors before guessing.
Done when you can apply the three questions to CPU, memory and disk.

tickets.title: Profile a slow Python service and name the real bottleneck
tickets.text:
Write `slow_service.py` with two functions: one burns CPU in a loop, the other waits with `time.sleep` as if it were waiting on the network. Run it under py-spy and read the profile. Add py-spy's `--idle` option, otherwise the sleeping function is hidden because it is not running; with `--idle` it shows up as waiting. On macOS py-spy may need `sudo`; if that is a problem, cProfile is the fallback (it shows the sleep as time spent in `time.sleep`).
Check: the profile shows the CPU function as working and the other as waiting, and you can say which one more cores would speed up.
Done when you can state that in one sentence.
explain: How do you tell whether a slow request is waiting or working?
explainAnswers: Look at what the request is doing in a profile or trace: time in CPU code is working, time blocked on a lock, disk, network or sleep is waiting. Compare CPU time with wall-clock time; if wall-clock is much larger, it is waiting. The fix differs: work needs faster code or more cores, waiting needs fewer or shorter waits.

tickets.title: Serve the simulator in front of a fake OpenAI-style endpoint
tickets.text:
Write a small HTTP server (standard library or a framework you know) with `POST /v1/chat/completions` that runs the request through the simulator and returns the completion after the simulated time (no streaming yet; the text can be filler words). Run the simulator in a background thread on a real-time clock (SimPy has a real-time environment, or sleep until each event) and let the handler wait for its request to finish. The prompt length is the word count of the message and the output length is `max_tokens`.
Check: a client that uses the standard OpenAI Python library, with its base URL pointed at your server, gets a completion for a request of 100 prompt words and 100 output tokens, and the response time is within 5% of the simulated finish time (about 2.1 s, so about 100 ms of room for the HTTP calls).
Done when the check passes.

tickets.title: Stream the tokens as server-sent events
tickets.text:
Make the endpoint stream when the request has `stream: true`: one server-sent-events chunk per simulated token, each sent at its simulated time, then a final `data: [DONE]` line.
Check: for a request of 8,000 prompt words and 20 output tokens, the time to the first chunk is within 5% of the simulated time to first token (1.12 s, so about 55 ms of room), and the number of chunks that carry a token equals the output length (the `[DONE]` line does not count).
Done when the check passes.

tickets.title: Skim the inference glossary, then write 15 terms from memory
tickets.text:
Skim Appendix A for 10 minutes. Then close it and write one sentence each, in your own notes, for: prefill, decode, TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, goodput, KV cache, continuous batching, prefix caching, PagedAttention, GQA, tensor parallelism, quantisation (W4A16 versus W8A8), speculative decoding and disaggregated serving.
Done when you can give all 15 in one sentence each without looking.
explain: Will a 70-billion-parameter model fit on one 80 GB GPU with 16-bit numbers? Show the sum.
explainAnswers: No. 70 billion weights times 2 bytes is about 140 GB, which is almost twice the 80 GB of memory, before any KV cache. It fits only if you shrink the weights (8-bit is about 70 GB, still too tight with a cache) or split the model over two or more GPUs.

tickets.title: Add fault switches: spikes, 5xx and slow streams
tickets.text:
Add three switches, as environment variables or query parameters: a latency spike (every Nth request is 10 times slower), random HTTP 500 errors at a set rate, and a slow stream (the delay between tokens is 5 times longer). Run your benchmark script from the T06 tickets against the server once with every switch off and once for each switch on, with short requests (20 prompt words, 20 output tokens) at 5 a second for 20 seconds. Add a p99 and a tokens-per-second line to `bench.py` if it lacks them.
Check: with a spike on every 10th request the p99 time to first token is higher than in the clean run; with errors at a rate of 20% the 100 requests include at least one HTTP 500 (the chance of none is about two in ten billion); with the slow stream the tokens per second are lower than in the clean run.
Done when all three effects show up.

tickets.title: Sweep arrival rates and emit TTFT, ITL, throughput and goodput
tickets.text:
First estimate the capacity in requests a second from the roofline numbers. Use a KV budget of 10 GB and lengths with medians of 1,000 prompt and 300 output tokens, either fixed or spread with a lognormal sigma of at most 0.3. Requests running together = KV budget divided by ((mean prompt + mean output tokens) x 163,840 bytes per token), using the mean lengths your generator really produces. Step time = the decode step time with that many requests running, each holding its prompt plus half its output tokens in the KV cache. The time one request needs in the shared batch = its prefill time + output tokens x step time / requests running together. Capacity = 1 divided by the mean of that time over the requests (about 3.4 requests a second for fixed lengths).
`make run` then sweeps the open-loop arrival rate from 10% to 120% of that estimate in 12 steps of 10%, sends 2,000 requests at each rate, lets every request finish, and writes a CSV: rate, p50 and p99 time to first token, p50 and p99 inter-token latency, throughput, goodput. A request's inter-token latency is its mean gap between tokens. Goodput counts requests that meet both targets (time to first token at most 500 ms and inter-token latency at most 50 ms; make the targets parameters).
Done when the CSV shows latency bending upward as the rate nears capacity.

links.label: NVIDIA, Benchmarking LLM inference at scale with AIPerf

tickets.title: Write the check: bound and Little's law
tickets.text:
`make check` asserts two things from the sweep, and records both in `results.json`. First, throughput never exceeds the memory-bandwidth bound: the largest batch your KV budget allows x 3.35e12 / 70e9 tokens a second. Second, Little's law holds within 5% at every rate: L, the time-average number of requests in the system, equals the arrival rate x W, the mean time in the system. Measure over the whole run, from time 0 until the last request finishes, and use the measured arrival rate (arrivals divided by the run length), not the nominal one; then the two sides agree to rounding, and the check catches bookkeeping mistakes such as a request counted in flight after it finished.
Done when both pass.

tickets.title: Write the check: knee and variance
tickets.text:
Add two checks. First, the knee: the lowest swept rate at which the p99 time to first token is at least 3 times its value at the lowest rate. It must lie between 50% and 110% of the capacity your formula predicts. Treat the engine as one server whose service rate is your capacity estimate, as in the T07 queue: waiting grows without bound as arrivals approach that rate, and in practice starts a little earlier because requests vary in length. If the knee comes out below 50%, the capacity formula is missing something (the prefill is a likely suspect): fix the formula, not the threshold. Second, variance: rerun the 30% step with another seed and 2,000 requests, keeping the length spread from the previous ticket (fixed lengths, or lognormal sigma at most 0.3; a wider spread can make two correct runs differ by more than 10%); the median time to first token changes by less than 10%. Print both medians.
Done when all checks pass and `results.json` records them.

tickets.title: Write one page on the tokensim design and what it taught you
tickets.text:
Write one page for a teammate who will extend it: what the simulator models and what it leaves out, the three numbers it reproduced from the maths, the surprise (where the sweep disagreed with your formula at first and why), and what you would build next.
It is graded against the design rubric: requirements and numbers, trade-offs, and what a stronger version would do.
Done when the page is in the write-up box.
explain: Why does the latency curve have a knee, and where is it?
explainAnswers: Below capacity requests rarely wait, so latency is nearly flat. As the arrival rate approaches the rate the engine can serve, queues build and waiting time rises steeply, which is the knee. In tokensim it sits close to the capacity set by memory bandwidth and the KV budget, and your queue formula should land near it, a little late because requests vary in length.

dsa_bank.topic: Graphs: BFS and DFS on grids and adjacency lists
dsa_bank.note: Write BFS and DFS templates from memory first: iterative and recursive, on a grid and on an adjacency list. Then the problems.
Kahn's algorithm and DFS post-order, both from memory. Know how to detect a cycle with each.

problems.name: Find All Possible Recipes from Given Supplies
Largest Color Value in a Directed Graph
Sort Items by Groups Respecting Dependencies

dsa_bank.note: Path compression and union by rank from memory. Know when union-find beats DFS: dynamic connectivity and Kruskal.

problems.name: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column
Min Cost to Connect All Points

dsa_bank.topic: Advanced graphs: shortest paths, MST, bridges, Eulerian paths
dsa_bank.note: Dijkstra with a heap, Bellman-Ford, Prim, Kruskal, Tarjan's bridges, Hierholzer. Fiset's playlist is the source; write each once from memory before the problems.

problems.name: Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination
Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in MST

dsa_bank.topic: Trees: DFS returns, path problems, BST properties
dsa_bank.note: Every tree problem is 'what does the recursive call return, and what does the parent do with it'. Write that sentence before coding each one.

problems.name: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
Kth Smallest Element in a BST
Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder
Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree

dsa_bank.topic: Trees II: views and orders, tries, segment trees and BIT
dsa_bank.note: Implement a trie, a segment tree with point update and range query, and a Fenwick tree from memory. Then the problems.

problems.name: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree
Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
Amount of Time for Binary Tree to Be Infected
Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

dsa_bank.note: For each: write the recursion with memo first, then tabulate, then space-optimize. Striver's series does exactly this order; follow it.

dsa_bank.topic: Dynamic programming II: 2-D grids and two-string DP
dsa_bank.note: Draw the table for every problem before coding. The bug is always the boundary row or column.

qbank.question: Describe one training step of a neural network in four moves. What changes at the end of it?
qbank.answer: Run a batch forward through the network to get predictions. Compare them with the targets using a loss function to get one number. Run backpropagation to get the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. Let the optimiser use those gradients to nudge each weight. The only thing that changes is the weights (and the optimiser's own state, such as Adam's running averages). The data and the network layout stay the same.
checklist: Only weights and optimiser state change

qbank.question: Why does a network need a non-linear activation function between its linear layers?
qbank.answer: Without a non-linearity, a stack of linear layers is still one linear layer. Multiplying matrices together gives another matrix, so extra depth adds nothing and the network can only draw straight-line boundaries. A non-linearity such as ReLU or GELU between the layers lets each layer build on the last, so the network can fit curved, complex functions. Transformers use it inside the feed-forward block of every layer.
checklist: Product of matrices is one matrix
Where it sits in a transformer layer

qbank.question: A 7-billion-parameter model is stored as fp32, bf16 and int8. How many GB is each file, ignoring metadata? Then roughly how much memory does full training with Adam in mixed precision need?
qbank.answer: Size is parameters times bytes. fp32 is 4 bytes: 7e9 x 4 = 28 GB. bf16 is 2 bytes: 14 GB. int8 is 1 byte: 7 GB. Mixed-precision training with Adam commonly keeps per parameter: 2 bytes bf16 weights, 2 bytes gradients, 4 bytes fp32 master weights, 4 bytes first moment, 4 bytes second moment = 16 bytes. So 7e9 x 16 = 112 GB, before activations.
checklist: 16 bytes per param for Adam mixed precision
qbank.source: https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054 (ZeRO paper, memory model: 2+2+12 bytes per parameter)

qbank.question: fp16 and bf16 are both 16 bits. Why do large-model training runs usually prefer bf16?
qbank.answer: They split the 16 bits differently. fp16 has 5 exponent bits and 10 mantissa bits, so it is more precise but its largest value is about 65,504 and small gradients can underflow; it needs loss scaling to train safely. bf16 has 8 exponent bits (the same range as fp32) and 7 mantissa bits, so it rarely overflows or underflows but is coarser. Training tolerates coarse numbers better than it tolerates overflow, so bf16 is the simpler default.
checklist: bf16 has fp32 range, less precision
Why range matters more in training

qbank.question: In one attention head, what are the query, key and value, and what does the softmax run over?
qbank.answer: Each token's hidden vector is projected three ways. The query says what this token is looking for, the key says what each token offers, and the value is the content that gets passed on. A token's query is dotted with every allowed token's key, scaled by the square root of the head dimension, and the softmax runs over those scores to give weights that sum to 1. The output is the weighted sum of the values. In a decoder the mask hides future tokens.
checklist: Three projections of the hidden vector

qbank.question: A model has 32 heads and you run a prompt of 8,192 tokens. If a layer built the full attention score matrix in fp16, how big would it be per layer? What does FlashAttention do about it?
qbank.answer: The scores are one 8,192 x 8,192 matrix per head: 67,108,864 entries. Times 32 heads is 2,147,483,648 entries, times 2 bytes is 4,294,967,296 bytes, which is 4 GiB for one layer. FlashAttention never writes that matrix to GPU memory. It splits the work into tiles that fit in fast on-chip memory and keeps running softmax totals, so memory use grows linearly with length and there are far fewer slow memory reads and writes.
checklist: Memory traffic, not FLOPs, is what it saves

qbank.question: Multi-head, grouped-query and multi-query attention differ in how many key/value heads they keep. What do you trade, and how much KV cache does it save for 32 query heads sharing 8 KV heads?
qbank.answer: Multi-head attention gives every query head its own key and value head. Multi-query shares one KV head across all query heads. Grouped-query attention is the middle: groups of query heads share a KV head. With 32 query heads and 8 KV heads the KV cache is 32/8 = 4 times smaller than multi-head, and decode reads 4 times less KV per step. The cost is a small quality loss that grouped-query keeps close to multi-head and multi-query does not always.
checklist: Less memory read per decode step

qbank.question: Why does prefill cost grow with the square of the prompt length, while each decode step with a KV cache grows only linearly with the context?
qbank.answer: In prefill every token attends to every earlier token, so n tokens need about n^2/2 query-key pairs. In decode the keys and values of earlier tokens are cached, so a new token needs only one query against n cached keys: n pairs, linear in context. The dense layers still cost the same per token either way. For short contexts the dense layers dominate, so total cost looks linear. The quadratic term takes over as prompts get long.
checklist: Decode: one query against n cached keys
Dense layers are linear in tokens
When the quadratic term starts to matter

qbank.question: What is a token, and why is the token count of a prompt not the same as its word count?
qbank.answer: A token is a chunk of text the model reads and writes: a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a space. A tokenizer, learned from data (often byte-pair encoding), splits text into these chunks. Common English words are often one token, but rare words, code and non-English text split into more pieces. A rough rule for English is about 0.75 words per token. Pricing, context limits and speed are all measured in tokens.
checklist: Rare words, code, other languages cost more
About 0.75 words per token in English

qbank.question: Pretraining compute is roughly 6 x parameters x tokens. For an 8B-parameter model trained on 15 trillion tokens, how many FLOPs is that, and how many GPU-hours at a sustained 400 TFLOPS per GPU?
qbank.answer: 6 x 8e9 x 15e12 = 7.2e23 FLOPs. At 4e14 FLOPs per second per GPU that is 7.2e23 / 4e14 = 1.8e9 GPU-seconds, which is 500,000 GPU-hours. On 2,048 GPUs that is about 10 days. 400 TFLOPS is roughly 40% of an H100's dense bf16 peak of 989 TFLOPS. Published runs report more hours than this, because of lower utilisation, restarts and evaluation.
checklist: Divide by sustained, not peak, FLOPS
Real runs cost more: restarts, lower utilisation

qbank.question: Your team wants a model to answer questions about internal documents. When do you fine-tune, when do you use retrieval, and when do you just put the text in the prompt?
qbank.answer: Prompt stuffing is the cheapest start when the material fits in the context and changes rarely, but you pay for those tokens on every call. Retrieval fits when the corpus is large or changes often: you can update documents without training and show sources. Fine-tuning changes behaviour, style or format and teaches stable skills; it is a poor way to add facts that change, and each update needs a training and evaluation cycle. Many systems combine retrieval with a light fine-tune.
checklist: Fine-tune: behaviour and format, not fresh facts

qbank.question: Why does RLHF with PPO need several models in GPU memory at once, and how does DPO change that?
qbank.answer: PPO-based RLHF keeps four models: the policy being trained, a frozen reference copy to limit drift (KL penalty), a reward model that scores outputs, and a value model (critic) for advantage estimates. It also generates text during training, so it needs an inference engine too. DPO skips the reward model, critic and online generation: it trains the policy directly on preference pairs with a loss that needs only the policy and a frozen reference. So it is far lighter, at the cost of less online exploration.
checklist: DPO uses preference pairs, policy plus reference

qbank.question: Define time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT). Which phase drives each, and which would you watch for a chat product versus a batch summariser?
qbank.answer: TTFT is the wait from sending the request to the first token arriving; it is dominated by queueing plus prefill, where the whole prompt is processed. TPOT (also called inter-token latency) is the gap between later tokens; it is set by decode steps. A chat product watches both: TTFT for responsiveness and TPOT for reading speed. A batch summariser mostly cares about total throughput and cost, so it can accept high TTFT and run large batches.
checklist: TPOT = one decode step as seen by one user

qbank.question: Decode for a single request on an 8B bf16 model reads all the weights each step. On one H100 (3.35 TB/s), what is the best-case tokens per second at batch size 1? Why is real life lower?
qbank.answer: Weights are about 8e9 x 2 bytes = 16 GB. Reading them takes 16e9 / 3.35e12 = 4.8 ms per step, so the ceiling is about 1 / 0.0048 = 209 tokens per second. Real speed is lower because the KV cache also has to be read, kernels do not reach peak bandwidth, and there is launch and sampling overhead. At batch size 1 the compute units are almost idle, which is why batching raises total throughput for free.
checklist: KV reads and overhead lower it
qbank.source: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/ (page lists 1,979 TFLOPS bf16 with sparsity; dense is half, 989)

qbank.question: If you double the decode batch size on one GPU, what happens to total throughput, to each user's token rate, and why?
qbank.answer: While decode is memory-bound, a step costs about the same whether it carries 16 or 32 sequences, because the weights are read once either way. Total throughput therefore rises almost 2x and each user's rate barely changes. As the batch grows, KV reads and then compute add time to each step, so steps lengthen and each user slows. Past the knee, more batch gives little extra throughput but a worse per-user experience, and queueing delay rises. The operating point is set by your latency target.
checklist: Throughput rises, per-user rate flat at first
KV reads and compute grow with batch
Pick the point from the latency target

qbank.question: One user sends a 100,000-token prompt to a shared server. Other users' streaming stalls. Why, and how would you fix it?
qbank.answer: A plain prefill runs the whole prompt in one forward pass that can last seconds, and decode steps for everyone else wait for it. The fix is chunked prefill: split the prompt into chunks of a few thousand tokens and mix each chunk with the running decode requests in the same step, under a per-step token budget. Decode users then see short, bounded delays. Another option is to send long prompts to separate prefill GPUs (disaggregation). Also add per-request limits and priorities.
checklist: Chunked prefill under a token budget

qbank.question: List the main things that occupy GPU memory when you serve a model, and say which one grows with the number of users.
qbank.answer: Model weights (fixed by parameter count and precision), the KV cache (grows with the number of tokens held across all active requests), activations and temporary buffers for the current step (small at inference), and runtime overhead such as the CUDA context and the memory allocator's slack. Weights are the same for one user or a hundred. The KV cache is the part that scales with users and context length, so it decides how many people fit.
checklist: KV cache is what scales with users

qbank.question: You serve a 70B model in 8-bit (70 GB of weights) on two 80 GB GPUs with tensor parallelism and a 0.9 memory limit. KV cache is 320 KiB per token. How many tokens of KV fit, and about how many 8K-token requests?
qbank.answer: Usable memory is 0.9 x 160 GB = 144 GB. After 70 GB of weights, 74 GB is left (ignoring activation and overhead, which take a few GB). KV per token is 2 x 80 layers x 8 KV heads x 128 x 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes (320 KiB). 74e9 / 327,680 is about 226,000 tokens. At 8,192 tokens each that is 27 requests, and fewer in practice after overhead.
checklist: KV per token = 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes

qbank.question: Can you fully fine-tune a 7B model with Adam on a single 80 GB GPU in mixed precision? Show the sum, and name two ways to make it fit.
qbank.answer: No. Mixed-precision Adam needs about 16 bytes per parameter (2 weights, 2 gradients, 4 master copy, 4 + 4 for Adam's two moments): 7e9 x 16 = 112 GB, which is already over 80 GB before activations. Ways to fit: parameter-efficient tuning such as LoRA (train small adapters, keep base weights frozen in bf16, about 14 GB), sharding states across several GPUs with FSDP or ZeRO, 8-bit optimisers, or offloading to CPU. Activation checkpointing helps the activation part only.

qbank.question: A 70B model must run on a single 80 GB GPU. Compare fp8 and 4-bit weights for how much KV cache is left, and say what quality risk you would test.
qbank.answer: At fp8 the weights are about 70 GB. With a 0.9 limit (72 GB), about 2 GB is left, which is roughly 6,000 tokens of KV at 320 KiB per token: barely one long request. At 4-bit, weights are roughly 38 GB including scales, leaving about 34 GB, around 100,000 tokens. So 4-bit gives real serving capacity, but weight rounding costs some accuracy, most visibly on reasoning and long-context tasks. Run your own eval on the task before and after, not just perplexity.
checklist: fp8 about 70 GB, leaves almost nothing
KV tokens left in each case

qbank.question: A laptop has about 200 GB/s of memory bandwidth. You run a 7B model quantised to 4 bits (about 4 GB). What tokens per second should you expect at best, and what does that tell you?
qbank.answer: Each decode step reads roughly all the weights: 4 GB. At 200 GB/s that is 4 / 200 = 20 ms per token, so a ceiling of about 50 tokens per second. Real runs land somewhat below it. It tells you local decode speed is set by memory bandwidth and model bytes, not by raw compute: halving the bytes (smaller model or lower precision) roughly doubles the speed.
checklist: Bytes read per token = model size
Bandwidth, not compute, is the limit

qbank.question: You start vLLM on a rented GPU. Which startup settings and log lines tell you how much KV cache you actually got?
qbank.answer: The engine loads the weights, profiles a forward pass to measure peak activation memory, then gives a share of the remaining memory to the KV cache. gpu_memory_utilization (about 0.9; 0.92 in recent releases) sets the overall cap, and max_model_len sets the longest sequence it must be able to hold. The startup log reports the KV cache size in tokens and the maximum concurrency for requests of the given length. If that number is small, lower max_model_len, quantise, or use a bigger GPU.
checklist: Log shows KV cache size in tokens
What to change if it is small

qbank.question: Running locally with a 4-bit model is free; a rented GPU with vLLM costs money. What does each teach you, and what does each hide?
qbank.answer: Local runs show real token speed, quantisation effects and memory limits at no cost, but the hardware is different from production: unified memory, no batching under load, and different kernels. A rented GPU with vLLM shows continuous batching, KV cache sizing and concurrency, which are the serving behaviours you will meet at work, but only for the minutes you pay for. Use local runs to learn the model's behaviour and the rented run to learn serving and measure scaling.
checklist: Local: cheap, real speed and quant effects
Local hides batching and production kernels
Cost limits the length of the run

qbank.question: Plan a 30-minute experiment on a rented GPU to see how tokens per second and latency change with load. What do you vary, what do you record and what would you conclude?
qbank.answer: Fix the model, prompt length and output length. Run an open-loop load at rising request rates, or closed-loop concurrency of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, for a few minutes each after a warm-up. Record TTFT and TPOT at p50 and p99, total output tokens per second, and GPU memory. Plot throughput against p99 latency. Throughput should climb then flatten while latency rises sharply at the knee. Report the load just before the knee as the usable capacity.

qbank.question: What is arithmetic intensity, and what does the ridge point of a roofline chart tell you for an H100?
qbank.answer: Arithmetic intensity is the number of FLOPs a kernel does per byte it moves from memory. The roofline caps speed by memory bandwidth at low intensity and by peak compute at high intensity. The ridge point is where the two meet: peak FLOPS divided by bandwidth. For an H100 SXM that is about 989e12 / 3.35e12, roughly 295 FLOPs per byte. A kernel below that is memory-bound, and above it compute-bound. Decode sits far below; large prefill sits above.
qbank.source: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/ (page lists 1,979 TFLOPS bf16 with sparsity; dense is half, 989) ; Williams et al., Roofline, CACM 2009

qbank.question: Prefill of a 2,000-token prompt on an 8B model: how many FLOPs, and what is the best-case time on an H100 (989 TFLOPS bf16 dense)? Ignore attention FLOPs.
qbank.answer: A dense transformer needs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token. So 2 x 8e9 x 2,000 = 3.2e13 FLOPs. At 989e12 FLOPs per second that is about 32 ms at peak. Real kernels reach maybe half of peak, so expect 60 to 80 ms. The 16 GB of weights are read once, taking about 5 ms, so prefill here is compute-bound rather than bandwidth-bound.
checklist: Compare with the 5 ms weight read

qbank.question: At what decode batch size does an 8B bf16 model on an H100 stop being memory-bound? State the simplifications.
qbank.answer: Each decode step reads the 2 bytes per parameter once and does 2 FLOPs per parameter per sequence. So intensity is about 2B / 2 bytes = B FLOPs per byte for batch size B. The ridge is about 295 FLOPs per byte, so the crossover is around batch 300. Simplifications: this ignores the KV cache reads (which grow with batch and context and push the real crossover lower in practice), attention compute, and imperfect kernel efficiency.
checklist: KV reads lower it in practice

qbank.question: Quantising weights to 4 bits speeds up decode a lot but barely helps a long prefill. Why? What would speed up prefill?
qbank.answer: Decode is limited by bytes read, so 4x fewer weight bytes shortens the step nearly in proportion. Long prefill is limited by compute. Weight-only quantisation still does the matrix maths in 16-bit after dequantising, so compute does not change and dequantisation adds a little work. To speed up prefill you need lower-precision maths too, such as fp8 or int8 for both weights and activations on hardware with those tensor cores, which roughly doubles peak throughput versus bf16.
checklist: W8A8 or fp8 changes the compute path

qbank.question: What are the three parts of a discrete-event simulator, and why use one for a serving system instead of a time-stepped loop?
qbank.answer: A clock, an event queue ordered by time, and state that events change. The loop pops the earliest event, advances the clock to its time, updates state and may schedule new events (a request arrives, a decode step ends). It skips idle time, so it runs far faster than real time and can simulate hours of traffic in seconds. Fixed time steps waste work when nothing happens and blur when events happen within a step.
checklist: Fast and repeatable with a seed

qbank.question: In tokensim you give the KV cache a 10 GB budget at 128 KiB per token. How many requests with a 2,048-token context can be held at once?
qbank.answer: 128 KiB is 131,072 bytes per token. 10e9 / 131,072 is about 76,300 tokens. Dividing by 2,048 tokens per request gives about 37 requests. If the simulator rounds each request up to whole 16-token blocks, a 2,048-token request uses exactly 128 blocks, so the answer stays 37. Real memory would be a little lower once you subtract activation and runtime overhead.

qbank.question: Sketch the core of tokensim: what is the per-step time model, how do requests enter, and what does it output?
qbank.answer: Model a decode step as max(weight-read time, compute time) plus a term for KV reads that grows with total cached tokens; model prefill time as tokens divided by a compute rate. Requests arrive from a seeded generator (Poisson or a replayed trace) with prompt and output lengths. A scheduler admits a request when its KV blocks fit, runs mixed steps, and frees blocks on finish. Output per-request TTFT and TPOT, throughput, queue length and KV usage so you can plot the latency knee.

qbank.question: Should the load generator be open-loop (arrivals at a fixed rate) or closed-loop (fixed number of users who wait for replies)? What does each show?
qbank.answer: Open-loop sends requests at a set rate whether or not earlier ones finished. When the server cannot keep up, the queue grows and latency explodes, which is how real public traffic behaves. Closed-loop holds concurrency fixed: when the server slows, users send less, so it hides overload (the coordinated omission problem) and reports kinder latencies. Use open-loop to find the capacity knee and closed-loop to model a fixed pool of clients, such as a batch job with N workers.
checklist: Choose by what real traffic looks like

qbank.question: Why can a KV cache be reused for a shared prompt prefix, and how does vLLM find a match?
qbank.answer: In a decoder, a token's keys and values depend only on the tokens before it. If two requests start with the identical prefix, the KV entries for that prefix are identical, so they can be computed once and shared. vLLM splits the cache into fixed-size blocks and gives each full block a hash of its tokens plus the hash of the preceding block. A new request looks up its block hashes; matching blocks are reused and only the rest is prefilled. A change anywhere in the prefix changes all later hashes.
checklist: KV depends only on earlier tokens

qbank.question: A request has a 4,000-token shared system prompt and a 100-token user message, on an 8B model. Compare the prefill FLOPs with a warm prefix cache and without. What is the ratio?
qbank.answer: Without caching, prefill covers 4,100 tokens: 2 x 8e9 x 4,100 = 6.56e13 FLOPs, about 66 ms at an H100's 989 TFLOPS peak. With the prefix cached, only 100 tokens are processed: 1.6e12 FLOPs, about 1.6 ms. The ratio is 4,100 / 100 = 41 times less compute. Real TTFT improves less, since queueing, scheduling and the attention over the cached prefix remain.
checklist: 2 x params x tokens each way
Attention still reads the cached KV

qbank.question: When does turning on prefix caching give you nothing or make things worse?
qbank.answer: It helps only when many requests share long identical prefixes. With unique prompts there is nothing to reuse, so you pay hashing and bookkeeping for no hit. A tiny change early in the prompt (a timestamp or user name at the top) breaks every later block. Cached blocks also occupy KV memory that running requests could use, so under memory pressure they get evicted before they are reused. Put stable text first, variable text last, and watch the hit rate.

qbank.question: Design a clean experiment to show prefix caching changed TTFT. What must you control?
qbank.answer: Use the same model, hardware and engine settings in two runs, one with caching off and one on. Use prompts with a long fixed prefix and short varying suffixes, at low concurrency so queueing does not mask prefill time. Warm up, then send many requests and record TTFT percentiles. In the cached run, check the hit-rate metric to confirm hits happened. Randomise order, repeat runs, and report medians with a spread. Also run a control with unique prompts, where caching should change nothing.

qbank.question: What is the difference between static batching and continuous (iteration-level) batching, and why does it matter for an LLM?
qbank.answer: Static batching groups requests, runs them together and waits until the slowest finishes, so GPU slots sit empty once short outputs end. Continuous batching schedules at every decode step: when a request finishes its slot is freed immediately and a waiting request joins at the next step. Output lengths vary widely, so this keeps the GPU full and cuts queueing delay. The Orca paper introduced it; vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM all do it.
qbank.source: Yu et al., Orca, OSDI 2022; https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180

qbank.question: Per-token KV is 128 KiB. A server reserves space for the maximum length of 4,096 tokens per request. A typical request uses 600 tokens. Compare with paging in 16-token blocks.
qbank.answer: Reserving for the maximum: 4,096 x 131,072 bytes = 512 MiB per request. Paged allocation rounds 600 tokens up to 38 blocks of 16, which is 608 tokens, or 76 MiB. So the reserved scheme uses about 6.7 times more memory for the same request, and on the same GPU fits roughly 6.7 times fewer such requests. The PagedAttention paper reports that earlier systems wasted a large share of KV memory through reservation and fragmentation.
checklist: Waste is internal fragmentation plus reservation

qbank.question: The KV cache is full and a higher-priority request arrives. Compare preempting a running request by swapping its blocks to CPU memory versus dropping them and recomputing later.
qbank.answer: Swapping keeps the work done: copy blocks to host memory over PCIe and copy back later. It costs transfer time (PCIe is slow compared with GPU memory) and needs spare CPU memory. Recompute frees the blocks at once and later re-runs prefill over the prompt plus tokens generated so far; that costs GPU compute, which is cheap for short contexts but wasteful for long ones. Swapping suits long contexts and spare host memory. Recompute is simpler and often fine. Either way, preemption should be rare.
checklist: Recompute: GPU cost grows with length
Which wins for long vs short
Choose the victim by priority or age

qbank.question: Design admission control for a KV cache so that requests do not get stuck halfway for lack of memory.
qbank.answer: When a request arrives, count the blocks its prompt needs plus a headroom estimate for output tokens. Admit it only if free blocks exceed that plus a watermark kept in reserve for running requests that need new blocks each step. Cap the number of running sequences. If memory still runs out, preempt the lowest priority or most recent request. Be conservative on admit and aggressive on queueing, and expose queue length and preemption count as metrics so you can tune the watermark.

qbank.question: What does each of data, tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism split? Which need a fast interconnect?
qbank.answer: Data parallelism copies the whole model on each GPU and splits the requests or batches. Tensor parallelism splits each layer's matrices across GPUs, so every layer ends with a collective such as all-reduce. Pipeline parallelism assigns different layers to different GPUs and passes activations along. Expert parallelism, for mixture-of-experts models, places different experts on different GPUs and routes tokens to them with all-to-all. Tensor and expert parallelism communicate every layer and need NVLink-class links; pipeline needs little; data parallel serving needs none between replicas.

qbank.question: Tensor parallelism across 8 GPUs on a 70B model (hidden size 8192, 80 layers, bf16). A decode step carries 32 sequences. Roughly how much data does each all-reduce move per GPU, and how many are there per step?
qbank.answer: Activation size per all-reduce is 32 x 8192 x 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes. A ring all-reduce moves about 2(N-1)/N of that per GPU: 1.75 x 524,288, about 0.92 MB. Each layer has two all-reduces (after attention and after the MLP), so 160 per step: about 147 MB of traffic per GPU. At hundreds of GB/s that is under a millisecond of pure transfer, but 160 small collectives each have fixed latency, so the latency per call matters more than the bandwidth.
checklist: Activation bytes = batch x hidden x 2

qbank.question: A model needs 16 GPUs across two 8-GPU nodes. Compare tensor parallelism across both nodes with tensor inside a node and pipeline between nodes.
qbank.answer: Inside a node, GPUs talk over NVLink at hundreds of GB/s. Between nodes the link is InfiniBand or Ethernet at roughly 50 GB/s per 400 Gb/s NIC, much slower and with higher latency. Tensor parallelism across nodes puts the per-layer all-reduce on the slow link, hurting every token. Tensor inside a node plus pipeline between nodes sends only one activation hand-off per stage over the slow link. The price is pipeline bubbles and a longer path per token, which batching can hide. The second layout is the usual choice.
checklist: Per-layer collectives on the slow link hurt
PP sends one hand-off per stage
Usual layout: TP in node, PP across

qbank.question: Plan how to serve a 405B-parameter model on 8 x 80 GB GPUs in one node. Does it fit, and what settings would you choose?
qbank.answer: At bf16 the weights are 810 GB, more than the 640 GB in the node, so it does not fit. At fp8 they are about 405 GB, which fits, leaving roughly 170 GB (after a 0.9 limit) for KV cache and overhead. Use tensor parallelism of 8 so every layer is split across the node's NVLink. Set max_model_len to what you really need to leave room for concurrency, check the KV tokens the engine reports, and test accuracy of the fp8 model on your tasks. For bf16 you would need two nodes.
checklist: Accuracy check; two nodes for bf16

qbank.question: How do GPTQ and AWQ differ from rounding each weight to the nearest 4-bit value?
qbank.answer: Plain round-to-nearest treats every weight alone and can damage accuracy at 4 bits. GPTQ quantises layer by layer using a small calibration set and second-order information, and adjusts the remaining weights to compensate for the error of those already rounded. AWQ observes that a small fraction of weight channels matter most, found from activation magnitudes, and scales them before quantising so they lose less precision. Both give much better 4-bit quality than rounding, at the price of a calibration step.

qbank.question: A draft model proposes k = 4 tokens and each is accepted with probability 0.8 (independently). On average how many tokens does one verification step produce? If the draft costs 10% of a target step per token, what is the speedup?
qbank.answer: With acceptance rate a and k drafted tokens, expected tokens per verification is (1 - a^(k+1)) / (1 - a). With a = 0.8, k = 4: (1 - 0.32768) / 0.2 = 3.36 tokens per step (the verification always yields at least one). The step costs one target pass plus four draft passes: 1 + 4 x 0.1 = 1.4 target-step units. Speedup is about 3.36 / 1.4 = 2.4 times. The independence assumption is a simplification.

qbank.question: When does speculative decoding slow serving down?
qbank.answer: It spends spare compute to save memory reads, so it helps when decode is memory-bound and batch size is small. At large batch sizes the GPU is already near compute-bound, and the extra verification work for rejected tokens costs real throughput. It also hurts when acceptance is low (a draft that disagrees with the target, or very creative sampling), when the draft is too big, and when it takes KV memory from the main model. Measure on production-like traffic at your normal load.

qbank.question: A vendor claims '4-bit, no loss in quality'. Design a short evaluation to decide whether to deploy it.
qbank.answer: Build a test set from your own tasks, with a few hundred examples and the metric you care about, plus a long-context and a structured-output slice. Run the full-precision and 4-bit models with the same prompts and settings, and compare scores with confidence intervals, not single numbers. Check refusals, formatting failures and output length changes. Measure speed and memory too, since the gain must be real. Roll out with a canary and keep a rollback to the original weights.
checklist: Own task set, not just perplexity
Speed gain verified; canary and rollback

qbank.question: What does a serving engine such as vLLM do that a plain model library script does not?
qbank.answer: A script loads a model and runs one request at a time. A serving engine adds the machinery for many users: continuous batching, KV cache management (paging and prefix reuse), an HTTP API with streaming, request queues and scheduling, tensor parallelism across GPUs, quantisation support and metrics. It keeps the GPU busy and memory under control while requests of different lengths come and go.

qbank.question: In vLLM, what do max_model_len, max_num_seqs, gpu_memory_utilization and tensor_parallel_size control?
qbank.answer: max_model_len is the longest sequence (prompt plus output) the engine accepts, and it sets how much KV memory it must be able to hold for one request. max_num_seqs caps how many sequences run in one step. gpu_memory_utilization is the share of GPU memory the engine may use in total; weights come first and the rest becomes KV cache. tensor_parallel_size is the number of GPUs a model is split across. Too-large lengths or caps shrink concurrency; too-high utilisation risks out-of-memory.
checklist: Effects on concurrency and OOM risk

qbank.question: Compare vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM for a team starting to serve open models.
qbank.answer: vLLM is the broadest default: wide model support, PagedAttention and prefix caching, an OpenAI-compatible API, and a large community. SGLang is also open source, with strong prefix reuse (RadixAttention) and structured generation, and does well on multi-call workloads. TensorRT-LLM compiles models into NVIDIA-specific engines and can reach the best speed on NVIDIA GPUs, but needs a build step, is tied to NVIDIA and is slower to adopt new models. Start with vLLM, benchmark on your own traffic, and switch only for a measured gain.
checklist: TensorRT-LLM: peak speed, build step, NVIDIA only

qbank.question: You must upgrade the serving engine version in production. Design the canary that proves it is safe.
qbank.answer: Replay recorded production requests (with consent and scrubbing) against the old and new versions side by side. Compare outputs on a fixed eval set for quality, since kernels and sampling can change; compare TTFT, TPOT, throughput and KV capacity at matched load; and compare error rate, memory and crash counts. Then shift a small share of live traffic to the new version with automatic rollback on error rate or latency thresholds. Pin versions in the image and keep the old one deployable.
checklist: Quality eval and perf at matched load

qbank.question: Explain streaming multiprocessors, warps, shared memory and HBM in a sentence each, and say which is the slow one.
qbank.answer: A streaming multiprocessor (SM) is one of the GPU's many small processors; an H100 has 132. A warp is a group of 32 threads that execute the same instruction together on an SM. Shared memory is a small, fast, programmer-managed memory on each SM. HBM (high-bandwidth memory) is the large off-chip main GPU memory: 80 GB on an H100, about 3.35 TB/s. HBM is the slow one relative to on-chip memory and compute, which is why kernels try to reuse data on chip.
checklist: Shared memory is small and fast
HBM is big and slow relative to chip

qbank.question: Compare the A100 80GB (312 TFLOPS bf16, about 2.04 TB/s) with the H100 SXM (989 TFLOPS bf16, 3.35 TB/s). How did the ridge point move, and what does that mean for decode?
qbank.answer: A100 ridge: 312e12 / 2.04e12, about 153 FLOPs per byte. H100: 989e12 / 3.35e12, about 295. Compute rose 3.2 times but bandwidth only 1.6 times, so the ridge point nearly doubled. More of the workloads fall below the ridge, so they are memory-bound on H100. Decode, already memory-bound, gains only about 1.6 times from the hardware change, while prefill gains up to 3 times. Batching more to use idle compute becomes more valuable.
qbank.source: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/ (page lists 1,979 TFLOPS bf16 with sparsity; dense is half, 989) ; https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/a100/

qbank.question: What problem does FlashAttention solve, and why is it called IO-aware?
qbank.answer: Standard attention writes the full n x n score matrix to HBM, applies softmax, then reads it back, so most of its time is memory traffic, not maths. FlashAttention computes attention in tiles that fit in on-chip SRAM, keeping running softmax statistics so it never stores the whole matrix. The result is mathematically the same attention with far fewer HBM reads and writes and memory that grows linearly in sequence length. It is IO-aware because the design counts memory movement between levels as the main cost.

qbank.question: When is it worth writing a custom GPU kernel, and when should you rely on libraries or the compiler?
qbank.answer: Libraries (cuBLAS, FlashAttention, CUTLASS) and compilers (torch.compile, Triton) already cover the common cases and improve with each release, so start there. A custom kernel is worth it when profiling shows one operation dominates, a fusion of several steps would avoid memory round trips, and no existing kernel handles your shape, dtype or layout. The costs are engineering time, hardware-specific tuning, correctness testing and maintenance on each new GPU generation. Profile first and estimate the gain before committing.

qbank.question: In a paged KV allocator, what is a block table and where does internal fragmentation come from?
qbank.answer: Each sequence has a block table: an ordered list mapping its logical positions to physical blocks in the cache, like a page table. Blocks need not be contiguous, so sequences can grow one block at a time with no big reservation. Internal fragmentation is the unused tail of a sequence's last block, up to block_size minus 1 tokens. Because it is bounded per sequence, waste is small and predictable, unlike reserving the maximum length up front.
checklist: Grow one block at a time
Waste only in the last block

qbank.question: Define the API of the block allocator in kvlab: what operations, what state, and what invariants?
qbank.answer: State: a free list of block IDs, a reference count per block, and a block table per sequence. Operations: Allocate(seq, n) takes n blocks from the free list or returns an error; Append for growth; Free(seq) decrements counts and returns blocks reaching zero; Fork(seq) copies the table and increments counts so children share blocks, with copy-on-write before a shared block is changed. Invariants: every block is either free or has a count above zero, never both; counts equal the number of tables referencing it; total blocks stay constant.

qbank.question: At 128 KiB per token, what is the average internal fragmentation per sequence with a block size of 16 tokens versus 128 tokens?
qbank.answer: On average the last block is half full, so the wasted space is about block_size / 2 tokens. For 16-token blocks that is 8 tokens x 128 KiB = 1 MiB per sequence. For 128-token blocks it is 64 tokens x 128 KiB = 8 MiB per sequence. With 200 concurrent sequences that is 200 MiB versus 1.6 GiB. Larger blocks waste more memory but reduce table size and allow more efficient memory access in kernels, which is the other side of the trade-off.
checklist: Larger blocks: fewer lookups, better access

qbank.question: How should a prefix cache evict blocks, and why can it only evict some of them?
qbank.answer: Only blocks with a reference count of zero (no running sequence uses them) may be evicted; blocks in use must stay. Among those, a common policy is LRU, and leaf-first for a tree of prefixes, because evicting a shared early block would make all later blocks that depend on it unreachable. When a free block is reused, remove its hash from the lookup table so a stale hash cannot match. Track hit rate: if hits are low, caching is just taking memory.

qbank.question: What are the parts of an agent harness around the model, and what does each do?
qbank.answer: The harness is the program that turns a model into an agent. It runs the loop: send messages and tool definitions to the model, read the reply, execute any tool calls, append the results, repeat until the model stops or a limit hits. Around that sit the tools themselves (file edit, shell, search), a permission layer that decides what may run, context management (trimming, summarising, caching), a sandbox, logging of every step, and limits on turns, time and spend. The model chooses; the harness enforces.

qbank.question: An agent starts with 5,000 tokens of system prompt and tool definitions, and each turn adds 2,000 tokens of tool output and reply. Over 30 turns, how many input tokens are sent in total? How does prompt caching change the bill?
qbank.answer: Turn i sends 5,000 + 2,000 x (i - 1) tokens. Summing over 30 turns: 30 x 5,000 = 150,000 for the fixed part, plus 2,000 x (0 + 1 + ... + 29) = 2,000 x 435 = 870,000. Total about 1.02 million input tokens, though the final context is only 63,000 tokens. Cost grows with the square of the number of turns because every turn resends everything. With prompt caching, the repeated prefix is billed at a fraction (Anthropic bills cache reads at a fraction of the base input price, 10% for many models), which cuts the bill sharply.
checklist: Caching bills the repeated prefix at a discount

qbank.question: When is a multi-agent setup (an orchestrator with sub-agents) worth its extra cost over one agent in a loop?
qbank.answer: Sub-agents help when the work splits into independent parts that can run in parallel, or when each part would otherwise flood the main context with detail. Anthropic reported that agents use about 4 times the tokens of a chat and multi-agent systems about 15 times, so the task must be valuable enough to pay for that. They are a poor fit when steps depend on each other or when all agents need the same shared context. Start with one agent and split only when you see the context or time limit bite.

qbank.question: A coding agent runs for hours and its context fills up. Design how the harness keeps it useful.
qbank.answer: Combine several techniques. Clear or truncate old tool results once they have served their purpose, since raw file dumps are the biggest consumer. When usage nears a threshold, ask the model to summarise the work so far (goals, decisions, files touched, next steps) and restart with that summary. Let the agent keep notes or a progress file outside the context so state survives. Send exploratory work to sub-agents that return short summaries. Keep the system prompt stable so it stays cached. Test that a resumed session still finishes the task.
checklist: Summarise and restart at a threshold

qbank.question: Break an eval into its parts and name one source of measurement error in each.
qbank.answer: An eval has a dataset of tasks, a harness that runs the model on them (prompts, tools, time limits, hardware), a grader that scores outputs (exact match, tests or a judge), and a metric that combines scores. Errors: a small or unrepresentative dataset gives sampling noise; the harness can change results through timeouts, resource limits or prompt format; graders can be wrong or biased; the metric can hide variance. Sampling randomness in the model adds noise on top, so one run is one draw.

qbank.question: A model scores 60% on a 200-question eval. What is the standard error, and what is a 95% interval? Another model scores 64%. Can you say it is better?
qbank.answer: Standard error of a proportion is sqrt(p(1-p)/n) = sqrt(0.6 x 0.4 / 200) = sqrt(0.0012) = 0.0346, so 3.5 points. The 95% interval is about plus or minus 1.96 x 3.5 = 6.8 points, so 53% to 67%. A 4-point gap is well inside that noise, so no, you cannot conclude it. Better: compare the models on the same questions with a paired test, use more questions, and repeat runs.

qbank.question: Grade with code (tests, exact match) or with an LLM judge? What are the risks of each?
qbank.answer: Code graders are cheap, fast and repeatable, but only work where correctness can be checked mechanically, and a weak test lets wrong answers pass. An LLM judge handles open-ended answers but is slower and costs money, can vary run to run, and has known biases: preference for longer answers, for the first position and for its own model family's style. Use code graders whenever possible, use judges with a written rubric where needed, and calibrate the judge against a human-labelled sample.

qbank.question: The same model gets different agentic-coding scores on two clusters. Design the harness so scores become comparable.
qbank.answer: Make the environment part of the spec. Pin container images, dependency versions and seeds, and give every task fixed CPU, memory and wall-clock limits that do not depend on neighbours. Separate infrastructure failures (out-of-memory, timeouts caused by load, flaky network) from model failures and retry or mark them, rather than counting them as wrong answers. Run each task several times and report mean and spread. Log resource use per task. Finally run a reference model on both clusters periodically to detect drift.

qbank.question: What is a reinforcement-learning environment for an LLM agent, and why must each rollout get its own isolated copy?
qbank.answer: An environment is the world the agent acts in: a starting state (such as a repository and a task), tools to act with, and a reward function that scores the result. A rollout is one attempt from reset to scored end. Each rollout changes files and processes, so sharing one copy lets rollouts contaminate each other and makes rewards noisy or wrong. Fresh isolated copies, usually containers or microVMs, also contain risky code and allow thousands of rollouts to run in parallel.

qbank.question: You must run 100,000 sandboxed tasks, each taking 6 minutes of work and 20 seconds to start the sandbox, with 2,000 sandboxes running at once. How long does the whole batch take, ideally? What would make it longer?
qbank.answer: Per task: 380 seconds. Total work: 100,000 x 380 = 38,000,000 sandbox-seconds. Divide by 2,000 concurrent sandboxes: 19,000 seconds, about 5.3 hours. The startup is 20 / 380 = 5% of that. Longer in practice: tail tasks that take much longer, retries after infrastructure failures, rate limits on the model API, image pulls for cold nodes, and scheduling gaps. Plan 20 to 30% extra and watch the straggler tail.

qbank.question: How would you cut sandbox startup for thousands of tasks: pre-built images, snapshots or a warm pool? What does each cost?
qbank.answer: Pre-built images per task make startup predictable but cost storage and a build pipeline, and cold nodes must pull them. Snapshots of a booted environment (for example microVM snapshots) restore in milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds, but the storage is bigger and state such as clocks and random seeds must be reset. A warm pool of ready sandboxes hides startup completely but holds idle capacity that costs money and must be reset between uses. Choose by how many distinct environments there are and how bursty the load is.

qbank.question: In an RL environment where the reward comes from hidden tests, how do you stop the agent from gaining reward by cheating (editing tests, reading answers, calling the network)?
qbank.answer: Assume the agent will try. Keep graders and answer files outside the sandbox and run them after the episode on a copy of the final state. Mount test files read-only, or copy in fresh tests at grading time so edits are discarded. Block or allowlist network, and remove credentials. Check the final diff for changes to test or build files. Use held-out tasks to compare rewards, and read samples of high-reward rollouts to find new exploits. Treat each discovered exploit as a bug in the environment and add a regression check.

qbank.question: What is the difference between a response that is valid JSON and one that matches your schema? Why does the client need to check both?
qbank.answer: Valid JSON only means the text parses. Matching the schema means it has the required fields, with the right types and allowed values. A model can return perfectly parseable JSON that is missing a field, has a string where you expected a number, or invents an enum value. Your code will fail later in a confusing place if you only parse. Validate against a schema (Pydantic, Zod, Go struct tags plus checks) straight after parsing, so errors surface at the boundary with a clear message.
checklist: Missing field, wrong type, bad enum
Error message reusable in a retry

qbank.question: Suppose 5% of calls return output that fails validation, and a retry fails with the same 5% probability, independently. With up to 2 retries, what is the average number of calls per request, and the chance a request still fails?
qbank.answer: Calls: 1 always, a second with probability 0.05, a third with 0.05 x 0.05 = 0.0025. Expected calls = 1 + 0.05 + 0.0025 = 1.0525, so about 5% extra cost. Chance of failing all three: 0.05^3 = 0.000125, 0.0125%. The independence assumption is optimistic: if the prompt is what makes the model fail, retries will fail together, and the real failure rate is higher. Check by logging retry success rate.

qbank.question: Compare three ways of getting structured output: prompting and parsing with retries, JSON mode, and schema-constrained decoding.
qbank.answer: Prompting plus validation works with any model, but you pay for failures and retries. JSON mode guarantees parseable JSON but not your schema. Constrained decoding (a structured-output feature or a grammar in the serving engine) restricts the tokens the model may produce so the result always matches the schema, which removes most retries. Its limits: supported schema features vary, forcing structure can slightly reduce answer quality on hard reasoning, and it fixes form, not truth. Keep validation anyway for business rules.

qbank.question: Design the retry logic for the structured-output client. What should be retried, how many times, and what goes into the retry prompt?
qbank.answer: Keep two separate loops. For transport errors (timeouts, 429, 5xx) use exponential backoff with jitter and respect Retry-After. For validation failures, retry at most two or three times: first try a cheap local repair (strip code fences, trailing commas), then ask again with the original request, the bad output and the exact validation error. Do not retry on 4xx request errors. Record each attempt, tokens spent and the error, set a total timeout, and raise a typed error at the end so callers can decide.

qbank.question: List the steps of a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, and say which steps run once and which run per question.
qbank.answer: Once, ahead of time: split documents into chunks, turn each chunk into an embedding with an embedding model, and store text, vector and metadata in a database. Per question: embed the question with the same model, search for the nearest chunks (optionally filter or re-rank), place them in the prompt with instructions, call the model, and return the answer with sources. Poor results usually come from chunking or retrieval rather than from the generating model.
checklist: Embed the query with the same model

qbank.question: You store 1 million chunks as 1,536-dimension vectors in pgvector using the vector type (4-byte floats). How big are the raw vectors? How much with the half-precision type?
qbank.answer: Each vector is 1,536 x 4 bytes = 6,144 bytes (plus a few bytes of header), so 1,000,000 x 6,144 is about 6.1 GB. With halfvec (2-byte floats) it is about 3.1 GB. The table's text and an index come on top: an HNSW index over the same vectors adds a similar order of memory or more, and it performs best when it fits in RAM. So budget roughly 2 to 3 times the raw vector size for a fast setup.

qbank.question: How do you choose a chunk size? What goes wrong if chunks are too small or too large?
qbank.answer: Too small and each chunk lacks context, so retrieved pieces are fragments that do not answer the question; there are also more chunks to store and search. Too large and the embedding blurs several topics into one vector so matching gets worse, and you spend prompt tokens on irrelevant text. Start with a few hundred tokens, split on natural boundaries (headings, paragraphs), add a small overlap, and attach the title as context. Then tune using a retrieval eval, not intuition.
checklist: Too large blurs and wastes tokens
Start around a few hundred tokens

qbank.question: Design an evaluation that tells you whether a bad RAG answer came from retrieval or from generation.
qbank.answer: Build 50 to 100 questions, each with the passage that contains the answer. Score retrieval alone: recall@k (is the right chunk in the top k) and MRR (how high it ranks). Score generation given the right chunk by supplying it directly. Then score the whole system end to end. If recall@k is low, fix chunking, embeddings or search. If recall is high but answers are wrong, fix the prompt or model. Also check groundedness: are the claims supported by the retrieved text.

qbank.question: For an LLM API, which errors should a client retry, and how should it wait?
qbank.answer: Retry rate limits (429), overloads and server errors (5xx), and network timeouts, because they are usually temporary. Do not retry bad requests (400), authentication errors (401, 403) or content that violates rules, since the result will not change. Wait with exponential backoff and jitter so many clients do not retry in step, and honour the Retry-After header when present. Cap the number of attempts and the total time, and make sure a retry will not cause a duplicate side effect.

qbank.question: Your provider allows 400,000 tokens per minute counting input and output together. Each request averages 2,000 input and 500 output tokens. How many requests per minute and per second can you sustain? What if retries add 5%?
qbank.answer: Each request uses 2,500 tokens. 400,000 / 2,500 = 160 requests per minute, about 2.7 per second. If retries add 5% extra requests, the effective capacity for new work is 160 / 1.05, about 152 per minute. Limits are often counted differently (input and output may be separate, and some providers estimate output up front), so read the provider's rules and keep headroom of 10 to 20% below the cap.

qbank.question: Streaming versus waiting for the full response: what do you gain, and what new problems appear?
qbank.answer: Streaming shows the first tokens in a fraction of the total time, which makes long answers feel fast, and lets you stop early. The costs: you handle partial output; the connection can fail midway, so you must decide whether to retry from scratch or continue; proxies and load balancers may buffer or time out idle connections; structured output cannot be validated until the end; and moderation or post-processing works on pieces. Use streaming for human-facing text and wait for the full response for machine-facing JSON.

qbank.question: Design the client-side protections for a service that makes many LLM calls: concurrency, timeouts, limits and fallback.
qbank.answer: Use a concurrency limiter plus a token bucket sized below the provider limits, and cut concurrency when 429s appear (additive-increase, multiplicative-decrease). Set separate timeouts for connect, first token and total time, plus an idle timeout for streams. Use a circuit breaker that stops calls to a failing provider for a short time. Add a fallback to another model or provider for low-risk paths, and a queue with priorities so interactive traffic beats batch. Emit metrics for latency, tokens, errors and retries.

qbank.question: What are the three kinds of things an MCP server can offer, and who decides when each is used?
qbank.answer: Tools are actions the model can call (run a query, create a ticket); the model decides when to call them, usually with user approval. Resources are data the application can read and attach as context (files, records), which the host or user chooses to include. Prompts are reusable templates the user picks, such as a slash command. The protocol is JSON-RPC 2.0 between a client inside the host application and your server. Servers cannot act on their own: the host controls what reaches the model.

qbank.question: Should your MCP server run over stdio or over Streamable HTTP? What changes?
qbank.answer: Over stdio the host launches your server as a child process and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC on standard input and output. It is simple, needs no network or login, and suits a local tool for one user, but it runs with that user's rights and must be installed on each machine. Over Streamable HTTP each message is a POST to one endpoint, so one deployment serves many users and needs OAuth, TLS, rate limits and tenant separation. The current spec (2026-07-28) is stateless: no initialize handshake or session id, so any replica can answer. Start with stdio; use HTTP to share.

qbank.question: Design the tools for an MCP server that lets an assistant look at a company database. What do you expose, and what do you refuse?
qbank.answer: Expose a few narrow, read-only tools with clear names and typed inputs (for example, find_orders_by_customer, get_order) rather than one raw run_sql tool. Connect with a database role that has SELECT only on named views, so permissions are enforced by the database and not by the prompt. Cap rows and response size, add time limits, and return error messages the model can act on. Mask sensitive columns, log each call with who asked, and require approval for any write tool you later add.

qbank.question: Why is the text of a tool description a security concern, and what can a user or host do about it?
qbank.answer: The model reads tool names, descriptions and results as part of its prompt. A malicious or compromised server can put instructions in a description (tool poisoning) or in a result, and the model may follow them, for example to read another tool's data and send it out. A server can also change its descriptions after the user approved it. Mitigations: install only trusted servers, show and pin descriptions for review, require human approval for sensitive calls, keep tools least-privilege, and avoid one session combining untrusted content, private data and an outbound channel.

qbank.question: What are the parts of an eval harness with a CI gate, and what does 'gate' mean here?
qbank.answer: A set of test cases with expected behaviour (a golden set), a runner that calls the system under test with fixed settings, graders that score each output, a report with the aggregate score and the cases that changed, and a stored baseline from the last accepted run. The gate is a rule in CI: if the new score is meaningfully below the baseline, or a must-pass case fails, the build fails and the change cannot merge. It turns a quality opinion into a check that runs on every change.

qbank.question: You want to detect a 5-point drop in pass rate from 70% with 95% confidence and 80% power, comparing two independent runs. Roughly how many cases per run do you need? What reduces the number?
qbank.answer: For two proportions the sample size per group is about 2 x (1.96 + 0.84)^2 x p(1-p) / d^2. With p = 0.7 and d = 0.05: 2 x 7.84 x 0.21 / 0.0025, about 1,317 cases per run. That is large. Pairing the runs on the same cases usually cuts it a lot, because most of the variance comes from which cases are hard. Other ways: a bigger drop threshold, repeated runs, or a one-sided test.

qbank.question: Run the full eval on every pull request, or a small smoke set per PR plus the full set nightly?
qbank.answer: The full set on every PR gives the strongest protection, but costs money and time, and slow checks tempt people to skip them. A small smoke set (tens of cases, mostly deterministic) gives fast feedback on obvious breaks, while the full set runs nightly or before release, to catch subtler regression. Choose by the cost of one run, the change rate and the risk. Also trigger the full set automatically when prompts, models or retrieval code change.
checklist: Cost and time of each run
Full set nightly or on risky changes

qbank.question: Design the gate logic so it blocks real regressions but does not fail on noise.
qbank.answer: Order the checks. First run deterministic checks (format, schema, must-pass cases) with zero tolerance. Then compute the score on the full set with a confidence interval, using a paired comparison with the baseline. Fail only if the interval says the score is below baseline by more than an agreed margin. Rerun failing cases a few times to separate flaky from broken. Store the history, post a per-case diff in the PR, and allow an owner to override with a written reason.
checklist: History, diff and override with reason

qbank.question: What distance measures can pgvector use, and when does the choice not matter?
qbank.answer: pgvector has operators for Euclidean (L2) distance (<->), negative inner product (<#>), and cosine distance (<=>). Cosine looks only at direction, L2 at straight-line distance, inner product at both direction and length. If the embeddings are normalised to length 1, which many embedding models do, all three give the same ranking, so use whichever is fastest and make sure the index operator class matches the operator in your query. If they are not normalised, pick what the model's documentation recommends.

qbank.question: Compare HNSW and IVFFlat indexes in pgvector.
qbank.answer: HNSW is a layered graph: it gives better recall-for-speed, can be built on an empty table and handles inserts well, but builds slowly and uses more memory. IVFFlat clusters the vectors into lists and searches only the nearest few (probes): it builds faster and uses less memory, but needs data present before the build to choose good centres, and recall depends on the probes setting and degrades if the data drifts. Both are approximate. Default to HNSW unless build time or memory is tight.
checklist: IVFFlat: faster build, needs data first

qbank.question: A table has 20 million 768-dimension embeddings. How much space is the raw vector data with 4-byte floats and with 2-byte halfvec? Could it sit in 64 GB of RAM along with an index?
qbank.answer: Float4: 768 x 4 = 3,072 bytes per vector, so 20e6 x 3,072 = 61.4 GB. Halfvec: 1,536 bytes, so 30.7 GB. With float4 the raw vectors alone nearly fill 64 GB, so no: there is no room for an index, the database cache or other work. With halfvec the vectors fit, but an HNSW index adds more again, so it is tight. Options: halfvec or binary quantisation, fewer dimensions, sharding, or a dedicated vector store.

qbank.question: A search needs both keyword precision and meaning, with a filter such as tenant_id. Design the query path in Postgres.
qbank.answer: Run two retrievals: full-text search (tsvector with a GIN index) for exact terms, and vector search for meaning. Merge them with reciprocal rank fusion, which adds 1/(k + rank) per list, so no score scaling is needed. Optionally re-rank the top 50 with a cross-encoder. For the filter, note that a vector index applied first and then filtered may return fewer than k rows; use a partial or per-tenant index for large tenants, or recent pgvector iterative index scans, and check recall with the filter on.
checklist: Filter after ANN returns too few

qbank.question: What are the stop conditions for an agent loop, and why do you need more than 'the model says it is done'?
qbank.answer: The normal stop is the model answering without a tool call, or calling a dedicated finish tool. A harness also needs hard limits for when that never happens: a maximum number of turns, a wall-clock limit, a token or money budget, a repeated-action detector (same call three times), and an explicit kill signal. Models can loop, get stuck on an error or declare success falsely, and nothing in the loop will stop them without these checks.
checklist: Natural stop: no tool call or finish tool

qbank.question: Your agent reads files and each tool result is about 20,000 tokens. The model's context window is 200,000 tokens and the prompt starts at 10,000. How many such reads fit? What would you change?
qbank.answer: Space available is 200,000 - 10,000 = 190,000. Dividing by 20,000 gives 9 reads, with no room left for the model's own output or later turns, so in practice about 8. Changes: read only the needed range of the file (offset and limit), search before reading, truncate or summarise large tool results, clear old results once used, and have a sub-agent do exploration and report back.

qbank.question: Should your agent plan the whole task first and then execute, or decide each step after seeing the last result?
qbank.answer: Planning first gives a visible, reviewable path, helps with long tasks and lets you approve before anything changes, but the plan is made with incomplete information and may be wrong. Step by step (the ReAct pattern) adapts to what each tool returns, and handles surprises, but can wander and is harder to review. Most useful agents mix them: a short plan, then adaptive steps, with re-planning when a step fails or the facts change.

qbank.question: Design the permission layer for your agent harness's file and shell tools.
qbank.answer: Classify tools by risk. Reads inside the project directory run freely. Writes are allowed inside the working directory and logged. Shell commands run in a sandbox with no secrets in the environment, a timeout and capped output, and are matched against an allowlist; anything outside it, and anything destructive (delete, force push, network calls) asks the user. Resolve paths to block escapes through .. or symlinks. Save decisions per session, not forever. Log every call, argument and decision to the journal.
