qbank.question: What are shadow traffic, a canary and an A/B test when you change the model that serves a feature?
qbank.answer: Shadow traffic copies real requests to the new model but throws away its answers, so users are unaffected; you compare cost, speed and quality offline. A canary sends a small share of live traffic to the new model, watches metrics, and increases the share or rolls back. An A/B test splits users into groups to measure a business outcome (conversion, satisfaction) with statistical care, and usually runs longer. Shadow is safest, canary tests real impact with limited risk, A/B proves value.

qbank.question: Traffic is 20 requests per second and your canary gets 5%. To detect a 5-point drop from a 70% success rate you need about 1,300 canary requests. How long must the canary run? What if you need it in 15 minutes?
qbank.answer: The canary receives 20 x 0.05 = 1 request per second, so 1,300 requests take 1,300 seconds, about 22 minutes. In 15 minutes (900 seconds) at 1 request per second you get only 900 requests. To reach 1,300 in 900 seconds you need about 1.45 requests per second, so about 7.2% of traffic. Or replace the live test with a paired offline eval on the same cases, or use shadow traffic, where the sample is not tied to the live share.
checklist: Other levers: offline paired eval, shadow

qbank.question: The new model passed the offline eval. Why still run a live canary, and what do you look at beyond the quality score?
qbank.answer: Offline sets are small and old; real users send different, messier requests. A live canary reveals behaviour the set missed and system effects: latency (time to first token and total), error and timeout rates, token usage and cost per request, refusal rate, output length, tool-call failure, and downstream metrics such as retries, thumbs-down or escalations. A model can score better and still be slower, wordier or more expensive. Sticky assignment by user also avoids confusing people with flip-flopping behaviour.

qbank.question: Design the model-swap canary pipeline end to end, including how rollback works.
qbank.answer: Pin the old and new model versions by name in configuration, not 'latest'. Gate 1: run the golden set on both and require no significant regression. Gate 2: shadow traffic to compare cost, latency and judged quality. Gate 3: route 5% of live traffic by sticky hash of user id, with guardrails on error rate, latency, cost per request, refusals and the quality judge. If a guardrail trips, flip the routing flag back to the old model, which takes seconds and needs no deploy. Step to 25%, 50%, 100% with a bake time at each. Keep the old model available for a week.
checklist: Rollback by config flag; keep old model

qbank.question: You try a new model each week. What should you do the same way every time so the comparison means something?
qbank.answer: Use the same small set of prompts and tasks each week, written down in advance, covering your real work: a coding task, a summary, a long-document question, a tricky reasoning task. Use the same settings and tool access, and record the model name and version, date, cost and speed with the output. Judge against a short rubric before reading the other model's answer. Without a fixed set you only compare moods, and results from different weeks cannot be lined up.

qbank.question: Model A costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Model B costs $1 and $5. A daily workload is 2 million input and 0.5 million output tokens. What does each cost per day, and what quality gap would justify A? (Prices are made up for the exercise.)
qbank.answer: Model A: 2 x $3 = $6 for input, 0.5 x $15 = $7.50 for output, $13.50 a day. Model B: 2 x $1 = $2 and 0.5 x $5 = $2.50, so $4.50 a day. A costs 3 times more, $9 a day or about $270 a month extra. It is justified if the quality gap saves more than that: fewer retries, less review time, or errors avoided. Measure the gap on your tasks, for instance rework rate, rather than assuming.
checklist: Compare with value of saved effort

qbank.question: A new model is clearly better on your test tasks. What else decides whether you switch your daily tools to it?
qbank.answer: Cost per task and speed, since a better model that is three times slower or more expensive may not pay off. Reliability on your tools and long sessions, not only single answers. Switching costs: prompts tuned to the old model, saved context, team habits, and any evals that must be re-run. Availability, rate limits and data policy. A sensible approach is to switch one workflow first, compare for a week with your log, and keep the old model as a fallback.

qbank.question: Design your own small 'taste test' of ten tasks for comparing models. What goes in and how do you score it?
qbank.answer: Pick ten tasks from your work: two coding fixes with tests, a code review, a long-document question, a summary with a length limit, an ambiguous request where asking a question is correct, a task that needs a tool, a maths or logic puzzle, a writing edit, and a safety-relevant request. Write the expected result or rubric first. Score each 0 to 2 (wrong, partly, right) and note time and cost. Refresh two tasks every month so the set does not go stale or get memorised, and keep a record of scores by date.
checklist: Simple scoring plus time and cost

qbank.question: You read a post saying a new technique doubles speed. What do you check before saving it as a fact?
qbank.answer: Find the primary source: the paper, repository or release notes, not a summary of a summary. Check what was measured (which model, hardware, workload, batch size) and against what baseline, and who ran it. Note the date, since this field changes quickly, and write it into the note as 'claimed by X on date'. Look for independent reproduction. Only treat it as established once you or a neutral source has reproduced it. Save the claim with its source link and your confidence.

qbank.question: With 15 minutes a day, do you read many headlines or a few things in depth?
qbank.answer: Headlines are cheap and keep you aware of what exists, but they leave you without detail you can use. Depth builds understanding but covers little. A workable split: spend about 3 minutes scanning your list of sources, pick at most two items, read one properly and save one line for the other. Choose depth when the item touches your current phase or tools, and breadth when you only need to know it exists. Save a note for each item you read properly, or the time is lost.

qbank.question: Set up a note template for the daily AI pulse so that the notes can be searched months later.
qbank.answer: Each note: date, source title and link, source type (paper, release note, blog, social), the claim in one sentence, who made it, evidence seen (numbers and conditions), your confidence (low, medium, high), tags for the plan areas it touches, and 'act by' with the next step or 'none'. Put the date and 'claimed by' on every external fact, so old claims can be revisited. A weekly review turns the best five notes into an update to your own plan or a task.

qbank.question: A vendor publishes a benchmark chart showing its new model ahead. What questions do you ask about the chart?
qbank.answer: Which benchmark, version and subset, and could test data have leaked into training (contamination)? Which settings: prompt format, number of attempts, tools, thinking budget, and were they the same for every model? Who ran the competitor's numbers, and were they taken from old papers? Are there confidence intervals or only point scores, and do the differences exceed noise? Does the benchmark resemble your work? Prefer independent runs, and treat vendor charts as a hint to test, not a conclusion.

qbank.question: What must a training checkpoint contain to resume exactly, and why is the model weights file alone not enough?
qbank.answer: Besides the weights, you need the optimiser state (for Adam, the two moment estimates for every parameter, which are larger than the weights), the learning-rate scheduler position, the step count, the random-number generator states, and the data loader position so the run does not repeat or skip data. Without optimiser state the run restarts with a cold optimiser and loss spikes. In distributed training each rank saves its shard, plus metadata describing the sharding so the job can resume on a different number of GPUs.

qbank.question: Checkpointing takes 5 minutes and the cluster fails on average every 6 hours. Using the Young/Daly formula, what interval should you choose, and what fraction of time is wasted?
qbank.answer: Young/Daly: interval = sqrt(2 x C x MTBF). With C = 300 s and MTBF = 21,600 s: sqrt(2 x 300 x 21,600) = sqrt(12,960,000) = 3,600 s, one hour. Overhead per hour is C / T = 5 / 60 = 8.3% spent writing checkpoints, and the expected lost work is about T / (2 x MTBF) = 60 / 720 = 8.3%. Total waste is about 16.7%. Faster checkpoints cut this a lot: the waste scales roughly with the square root of the checkpoint time.
qbank.source: Young (1974); Daly, Future Generation Computer Systems 22(3), 2006

qbank.question: A large training run saw 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days. Estimate the MTBF in hours, and the best checkpoint interval if a checkpoint blocks training for 100 seconds.
qbank.answer: 54 days is 1,296 hours; 1,296 / 419 = 3.09 hours, or about 11,140 seconds. Young/Daly: sqrt(2 x 100 x 11,140) = sqrt(2,228,000), about 1,490 seconds, roughly 25 minutes. So failures arrive about every three hours and you checkpoint about every 25 minutes. Making checkpoints asynchronous shrinks the blocking time C, which shortens the best interval and the lost work. Figures are from the Llama 3 report, which described its 16,384-GPU run.

qbank.question: Compare writing checkpoints synchronously to a shared file system with writing to local NVMe or memory first and uploading in the background.
qbank.answer: Synchronous writes to shared storage are simple and durable, but every rank stops training while a very large amount of data is written, and the shared file system becomes a bottleneck at scale. Writing first to local NVMe or host memory takes seconds, then a background process copies it to durable storage while training continues, so blocking time falls sharply. The costs: the data is not safe until the copy completes, local copies are lost if the node dies, and the extra memory and complexity. A tiered scheme keeps frequent fast local checkpoints and fewer durable ones.

qbank.question: In data-parallel training (DDP) on two GPUs, what is replicated, what is split, and what is communicated each step?
qbank.answer: The full model and optimiser are replicated on both GPUs. The batch is split: each GPU takes different examples and computes its own gradients. Each step the GPUs average their gradients with an all-reduce, so both apply the identical update and stay in sync. Only gradients travel, once per step, and frameworks overlap the all-reduce with the backward pass to hide the cost. If one worker dies, the collective hangs or errors, which is what you will see when you kill it.

qbank.question: A 1-billion-parameter model has 2 GB of bf16 gradients. On two GPUs, a ring all-reduce moves 2(N-1)/N times the data per GPU. How long does the exchange take over a 10 Gbit/s link versus NVLink at 450 GB/s per direction?
qbank.answer: With N = 2 the factor is 1, so each GPU sends and receives about 2 GB. At 10 Gbit/s (1.25 GB/s) that is 1.6 seconds per step. Over NVLink at 450 GB/s it is about 4.4 milliseconds. If a step's compute is, say, 300 ms, the slow link makes the run mostly wait on the network, while NVLink makes communication almost free. This is why you check the rented machine's interconnect before paying for it.

qbank.question: Rent one machine with two GPUs or two machines with one GPU each?
qbank.answer: One machine with two GPUs has fast local links (NVLink or PCIe), one set of storage and networking, and simple setup. Two single-GPU machines show more realistic multi-node problems, such as network setup, rendezvous and a worker host failing independently, but they communicate over Ethernet, which is slow, and cost more setup time. For learning failure behaviour, the two-machine setup is closer to production; for learning the training mechanics cheaply, one machine is easier. Pick based on what you want to see.

qbank.question: Plan the two-GPU experiment so it stays inside budget and teaches you about failure.
qbank.answer: Rehearse everything on CPU first with the gloo backend and a toy model, so rented time is spent on GPU-specific things only. Script the launch, a checkpoint every N steps, and logging of step time and loss. Set an automatic shutdown timer and a budget alert before you start. On the rented machine run a baseline, then kill one worker mid-run and record what the other does (hang, timeout, error). Restart from the checkpoint and confirm the loss continues smoothly. Copy logs off the machine, then destroy it.

qbank.question: What do ZeRO stages 1, 2 and 3 (or FSDP) shard, and what does each cost in communication?
qbank.answer: Plain data parallelism keeps a full copy of weights, gradients and optimiser state on every GPU. ZeRO-1 shards the optimiser state across GPUs. ZeRO-2 also shards gradients. ZeRO-3, like FSDP full sharding, also shards the weights, gathering each layer just in time with an all-gather and releasing it after use. Stage 1 and 2 add little communication beyond the gradient reduction; stage 3 adds weight all-gathers in both forward and backward, about 1.5 times the traffic of plain data parallelism, in exchange for memory that falls with the number of GPUs.

qbank.question: With ZeRO-3 and mixed-precision Adam (16 bytes per parameter of state), how much state memory does each GPU hold when training a 70B model on 64 GPUs? Is that the whole memory need?
qbank.answer: Total state is 70e9 x 16 bytes = 1.12 TB. Sharded over 64 GPUs it is 1.12e12 / 64 = 17.5 GB per GPU. That is not the whole need. You also need activations (which depend on batch and sequence length and can be large without activation checkpointing), temporary buffers for the weights gathered for the current layer, communication buffers and the framework overhead. So the state fits comfortably in 80 GB, but the full budget has to be checked with a profile.

qbank.question: Fully sharded data parallelism or tensor plus pipeline parallelism for a large training job?
qbank.answer: FSDP is simple to adopt: the model code stays almost as written, and it scales memory across data-parallel GPUs, but it all-gathers weights across the network every step, so it is sensitive to bandwidth at large scale. Tensor plus pipeline (often with data parallel as well, called 3D parallelism) keeps communication local, with tensor parallelism inside fast NVLink nodes and pipeline across nodes, and reaches higher efficiency at very large scale, but needs careful model-specific partitioning and tuning. Start with FSDP, and add model parallelism when you hit scaling limits.

qbank.question: What is model FLOPs utilisation (MFU), how do you compute it and what is a good value?
qbank.answer: MFU is the useful model FLOPs per second you achieve divided by the hardware's peak FLOPs per second. Model FLOPs are counted from the maths of the model, about 6 x parameters per token for training, not from what the GPU actually executed. Tokens per second x 6 x parameters / (GPUs x peak FLOPs) gives the fraction. Large dense-model runs commonly report around 35 to 55%; the Llama 3 405B run reported roughly 38 to 43%. It is a quick way to spot an infrastructure problem.

qbank.question: Name the main collective operations and how all-reduce relates to reduce-scatter and all-gather.
qbank.answer: Broadcast sends one GPU's data to all. Reduce combines data from all onto one GPU. All-reduce combines and gives the result to every GPU. Reduce-scatter combines and leaves each GPU holding one piece of the result. All-gather collects each GPU's piece so everyone ends with the full set. All-to-all sends a different piece to each other GPU. An all-reduce can be built as a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, which is how ring all-reduce works and why sharded training uses those two operations directly.

qbank.question: A ring all-reduce of 10 GB of gradients across 8 GPUs. How long on NVLink (about 450 GB/s per direction) and across nodes over a 400 Gb/s (50 GB/s) NIC?
qbank.answer: The ring moves 2 x (N-1)/N x S = 2 x 7/8 x 10 GB = 17.5 GB through each GPU's links. On NVLink at 450 GB/s: 17.5 / 450 = 39 ms. Over a single 50 GB/s NIC: 17.5 / 50 = 350 ms, nine times slower. This ignores latency and the real bus efficiency, so measured times are longer. It shows why large jobs keep the heaviest traffic (tensor parallel) on NVLink and use many NICs per node, and why topology-aware collectives matter.

qbank.question: InfiniBand or RoCE (RDMA over Ethernet) for a GPU cluster fabric?
qbank.answer: InfiniBand is purpose-built for lossless, low-latency RDMA, with mature congestion control and tooling, and is the usual choice for the largest training clusters, but it is a separate network with a single main vendor and different operations skills. RoCE runs RDMA over Ethernet, so you reuse Ethernet switches, vendors and skills, and it can be cheaper and more open, but it needs careful configuration (priority flow control, ECN, congestion control) to avoid drops and head-of-line blocking. Meta has described building 24,000-GPU clusters on each of the two technologies.

qbank.question: Why does network topology and job placement matter for a collective, and what is oversubscription?
qbank.answer: A collective is limited by its slowest link. If the GPUs of a job sit under one leaf switch, traffic stays local and fast. If they are spread across racks, traffic crosses spine switches that other jobs share, so contention and extra hops slow every step. Oversubscription means the uplink capacity is lower than the total downlink capacity, for example 2:1; fine for mixed traffic, bad for synchronised all-reduce where every node sends at once. Schedulers therefore place a job close together and use rail-optimised layouts that connect matching GPUs on different nodes.

qbank.question: What kinds of GPU hardware faults happen in a large fleet, and how do they show up?
qbank.answer: Common ones: uncorrectable memory (ECC) errors, a GPU that drops off the bus (reported as an XID error in the kernel log), overheating and throttling that slows one GPU, NVLink or network link errors, silent data corruption that gives wrong numbers without any error, and host problems such as power supplies and disks. They show up as crashes, hangs in collectives, one GPU running slower than the others, loss spikes, or error counters in tools like DCGM. Silent errors are the hardest because nothing fails loudly.

qbank.question: The Llama 3 report: 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days on 16,384 GPUs. If the failure rate per GPU stays the same, how often would you expect an interruption on a 100,000-GPU cluster?
qbank.answer: Rate per GPU-day = 419 / (16,384 x 54) = 4.7e-4. For 100,000 GPUs: 100,000 x 4.7e-4 = 47 interruptions a day, one every 30 minutes. That means checkpoint and restart cannot take tens of minutes, and automation must detect, replace and resume without a person. Caveats: it is one run's data; rates change with hardware generation, age and burn-in; and not every interruption involves a GPU (about 58% were GPU-related in that report).

qbank.question: Should the fleet quarantine a node at the first suspicious sign, or wait for repeated errors?
qbank.answer: Quarantining quickly protects jobs from bad nodes and stops one flaky GPU from crashing job after job, but false positives remove healthy capacity, and capacity is expensive. Waiting preserves capacity but can waste many GPU-hours when a bad node interrupts large jobs. A middle policy: act immediately on severe signals (uncorrectable ECC, fell off the bus), use counts or rates for soft signals, run a short diagnostic on a drained node, and return it to the pool if it passes. Track false-positive rate and repeat offenders to tune the thresholds.
checklist: Counts or rates for soft signals

qbank.question: Design the health pipeline that keeps bad GPUs out of training jobs.
qbank.answer: Before each job: a quick check per node (DCGM diagnostics, memory test, a small multi-GPU NCCL all-reduce with a bandwidth threshold) before it joins. During jobs: collect telemetry (ECC counters, temperature, clocks, link errors, step time per rank) and flag stragglers. On a failure, a controller cordons and drains the node, labels the reason, and opens a ticket. A burn-in test runs on repaired nodes before they return. Keep a ledger of each node's history so repeat offenders go to hardware repair.

qbank.question: What are the parts of a progressive rollout, and what stops it?
qbank.answer: Split the target into waves of increasing size (for example one node, then 1%, 5%, 25%, the rest). Apply the change to a wave, wait a bake time to see problems that appear slowly, check health gates (error rate, latency, GPU health, eval score), and only then start the next wave. A failed gate pauses or rolls back the rollout. A limit on unavailable capacity (max-unavailable or a disruption budget) keeps enough nodes serving at all times. The wave and gate definitions are written down before the rollout starts.

qbank.question: You update 2,000 nodes, at most 5% at a time, and each batch takes 10 minutes to drain, update and verify. After a 1-node canary baked for 30 minutes, how long is the whole rollout?
qbank.answer: Five percent of 2,000 is 100 nodes per batch, so 2,000 / 100 = 20 batches (the canary node is part of the first). 20 x 10 minutes = 200 minutes. Adding the 30-minute canary bake gives 230 minutes, about 3.8 hours. If you add a bake time between batches, say 5 minutes each, add up to 100 minutes more. The limit of 5% unavailable is the throttle: raising it to 10% halves the batch time but doubles the capacity at risk.

qbank.question: Blue-green versus rolling updates for GPU model servers.
qbank.answer: Blue-green stands up a complete second copy, tests it, then switches traffic at once, with a very fast rollback. For GPU servers that means paying for double the accelerators during the change, which is rarely affordable at scale. Rolling replaces replicas a few at a time, using little extra capacity, but the old and new versions run together for a while and rollback means rolling back again. For GPU fleets, a rolling or canary update with a small surge is the usual choice, while blue-green fits small or critical services.
checklist: Rolling: low extra capacity, mixed versions

qbank.question: Design the gates for rolling out a new model version to a serving fleet.
qbank.answer: Pre-gates: the golden eval set passes with a paired comparison against the baseline, and a load test shows latency and memory within limits. During rollout, waves of increasing traffic share, each with a bake time. Gate metrics: error and timeout rate, time to first token and per-token latency, GPU memory and KV evictions, cost per request, refusal and format-failure rates, and a sampled judge score. Define thresholds before starting. On breach, stop and route traffic back to the previous version, which stays loaded or fast to restore. In-flight requests are drained, not cut.
checklist: Metrics for latency, errors, cost, quality

qbank.question: Which Prometheus metric types would you use in gpufleet for node health, rollout progress and request latency?
qbank.answer: Gauges for values that go up and down: a node's health state, temperature, GPUs free. Counters for things that only increase, such as rollout waves completed or errors seen; you query them with rate(). Histograms for latency, which give bucketed counts so you can compute percentiles with histogram_quantile across many instances. Keep label values low-cardinality (node pool, version, result) and avoid unbounded labels like request id.

qbank.question: gpufleet simulates 2,000 nodes with 8 GPUs and exports 20 metrics per GPU, scraped every 15 seconds. How many time series is that, and roughly how much disk per day if a sample costs about 1.5 bytes?
qbank.answer: Series: 2,000 x 8 x 20 = 320,000. Samples per series per day: 86,400 / 15 = 5,760. Total: 320,000 x 5,760 = 1.84 billion samples a day. At about 1.5 bytes each (Prometheus documents roughly 1 to 2 bytes per sample after compression) that is about 2.8 GB a day. Memory is the bigger limit, since each active series costs a few kilobytes: 320,000 series is well within a single Prometheus but shows why you drop unneeded per-GPU labels.

qbank.question: Design the node-health controller state machine in gpufleet.
qbank.answer: States: Healthy, Suspect, Cordoned, Draining, Repair, Burn-in, then back to Healthy. Inputs are health signals with severity. A severe signal moves Healthy straight to Cordoned; soft signals accumulate to Suspect and then Cordoned. Each reconcile reads the actual state, compares it with the desired state, and takes one idempotent step, so a restart changes nothing. Draining waits for work to finish within a timeout. Record every transition with its reason and time, and cap how many nodes may be out at once so the controller cannot drain the whole fleet.

qbank.question: Who decides to proceed in an eval-gated canary: a fully automatic gate, a human approval, or both?
qbank.answer: A fully automatic gate is fast, consistent and works at night, but trusts the metrics and the eval, which may miss a new kind of failure. Human approval adds judgement and accountability, but it is slow, depends on who is awake and can become a rubber stamp. A common design: automatic for the early, small waves with tight rollback rules, and a human approval before the step to broad exposure, with the evidence (scores with intervals, cost, sample outputs) put in front of the approver. Rollback should always be automatic.

qbank.question: What makes a task a good one to hand to an agent, and what makes it a poor one?
qbank.answer: Good tasks have a clear end you can check (a test passes, a file has the right shape), are bounded in size, are reversible (in a branch, with version control), and have context the agent can find in the repository. Poor ones are vague, depend on knowledge in your head, cannot be checked without lots of your time, are costly to undo (production data, sending messages), or involve a decision you should own. If you cannot say how you will know it is right, do not hand it off yet.

qbank.question: Should you let the agent run a long task on its own, or approve each step?
qbank.answer: Approving each step catches mistakes early and keeps you aware, but it wastes your time on routine steps and leads to rubber-stamping once you get tired. Letting it run saves time but allows a long wrong path, and a larger mess to clean up. Match the oversight to risk: let it run on safe, reversible work inside a sandbox or branch with checkpoints, and require approval before irreversible actions or changes outside the task. Review the result against the acceptance criteria rather than every keystroke.

qbank.question: Design the daily log for working with an agent, so it becomes useful after a month.
qbank.answer: One short entry per task: date, task, what you asked (link or paste), what you expected, what you got, what you had to redo and why, time spent by you and by the agent, and a tag for the cause (vague request, missing context, wrong tool, model limit, my change of mind). At the end of each week, group by cause and mark tasks as delegate, collaborate or keep. After a month, the counts show which request styles work and which tasks to stop handing over.

qbank.question: What is the role of a project instruction file such as CLAUDE.md, and what should and should not go in it?
qbank.answer: It is text the agent reads at the start of each session, so it carries conventions it cannot infer: how to build and test, code style, directory layout, rules like 'never touch X', and common mistakes. Keep it short and specific; long files get ignored or waste context. Do not put secrets, long documentation that belongs elsewhere, or things the code already shows. Treat it like code: review it, update it when the agent keeps making the same mistake, and prefer a concrete rule to a vague hope.

qbank.question: List the parts of a spec an agent can follow.
qbank.answer: The goal and why it matters; the context (where in the code, what exists); the requirements, in plain behaviours; constraints (what not to touch, libraries, style); non-goals, so it does not wander; acceptance criteria that can be checked; how to verify (commands to run); and when to stop and ask. Concrete examples of inputs and outputs help a great deal. The test of a spec is whether a competent stranger could do the work without asking you a question.

qbank.question: Turn 'make the login faster' into a spec an agent can act on.
qbank.answer: Goal: reduce the time from submitting credentials to the home page, for returning users. Context: login handler in auth/, session store in Redis, p95 now 1.8 s measured by the load script in scripts/. Requirements: find the slowest steps with a profile first and report them before changing code. Constraints: no change to the password hashing cost or security checks. Acceptance: p95 under 800 ms with the same script, all existing tests pass, no new dependencies. Stop and ask if the main cause is outside auth/.

qbank.question: Write a detailed spec up front, or let the agent explore first and then write the plan?
qbank.answer: A detailed spec up front prevents misunderstandings, but if you write it before you know the codebase it can be wrong in confident detail and costs you time. Letting the agent explore (read-only) and propose a plan first uses its speed to find facts, and you correct the plan before any code changes. For small, clear tasks go straight to the work. For larger or unfamiliar ones, explore, plan, review the plan, then implement, and put the agreed plan into a file the agent can re-read.
checklist: Cost of a wrong detailed spec

qbank.question: Why is it risky to let the same agent write the code and the tests that decide whether the code is right?
qbank.answer: The agent can write tests that match its own misreading of the requirement, so the tests pass and the work is still wrong. It can also weaken or special-case tests to make them pass. Independent checks are better: tests derived from the spec by someone or something that has not seen the code, held-out examples the agent cannot see, property checks, and your own review of the acceptance criteria. At least have the tests written first from the spec and review them before the implementation starts.

qbank.question: What are the dependency types that stop two agent tasks from running in parallel?
qbank.answer: Data dependency: one task needs the output of the other. File or resource conflict: both edit the same files, the same database, port or lock, so changes collide on merge. Ordering dependency: a schema or interface must exist before dependants can compile. Shared decision: both depend on an unresolved design choice. Fix by first agreeing the interface or schema, giving each agent its own files or branch (separate worktrees), and merging in a planned order. If you cannot define the boundaries, do it sequentially.

qbank.question: A single chat answer costs about $0.05. If agents use about 4 times the tokens and multi-agent systems about 15 times, what are the costs? When does the higher cost pay off?
qbank.answer: An agent run costs about 4 x $0.05 = $0.20 and a multi-agent run about 15 x $0.05 = $0.75, using the multipliers Anthropic reported for its research system. The bill is worth paying when the work saved is worth more: if the agent does what would take you 30 minutes, then $0.75 is cheap even at a modest hourly rate. It is not worth it for tasks a single answer could do. Measure your own multiples, since they vary a lot by task.

qbank.question: How do you choose between a small cheap model and a large one for each piece of work?
qbank.answer: Use the cheaper model for work that is routine, well specified and easy to check: renames, boilerplate, formatting, summarising, running and reporting tests. Use the stronger model where judgement matters: design, hard debugging, ambiguous requirements, and reviewing others' work. Starting cheap and escalating when the checks fail often works, but retries cost time. Test on a sample of your own tasks: if the cheap model's rework rate is low, the saving is real; if you redo its work, it is not.
checklist: Routine, checkable work to cheap models

qbank.question: Write the brief you would give a worker agent for one well-scoped piece of work.
qbank.answer: Goal and why. Exact files or directories it may touch, and those it must not. Decisions already made (interfaces, naming, libraries). Acceptance criteria that can be checked, with the exact commands that verify them. Output format: what to report, where to write results, and whether to commit. Stop conditions: report instead of improvising if the interface needs to change, tests cannot be made to pass, or the scope grows. The brief should stand alone, because the worker has none of your context.

qbank.question: List ways to verify work an agent did, from cheapest to most expensive.
qbank.answer: Read its final report and the diff summary; run the type checker, linter and tests yourself rather than trust 'all passed'; run the changed feature by hand; compare behaviour against examples from the spec; have a separate reviewer agent or person read the diff with fresh context; check against held-out cases the agent never saw; and, for risky changes, a staged rollout with monitoring. Match the depth to the cost of being wrong. Always check claims the agent makes about its own work, such as 'I ran the tests'.

qbank.question: Is it enough to ask the same model to review its own work?
qbank.answer: It catches some slips, such as typos, missed requirements and obvious bugs, especially in a fresh session with the spec and diff but not the earlier reasoning. But the same model shares the same blind spots and tends to approve what it wrote, so errors born of a misunderstanding survive. A different model, or a different prompt that checks specific risks, adds some independence; deterministic checks (tests, types, linters) add more; a human on the risky parts adds the most. Use self-review as a first filter, never the only one.

qbank.question: Design the checks that a pull request from an agent must pass before you merge it.
qbank.answer: Automated: build, lint, types, the full test suite, a check that no test files were weakened or deleted, and a diff-size limit. Evidence: the agent states which commands it ran with output, and the CI log confirms it. Review: you read the diff for the risky areas (security, data, public interfaces), spot-check two claims in the description against the code, and try the main behaviour once. Hold-out: run a small set of cases the agent did not see. Record outcome and rework in your log.

qbank.question: Name four ways an agent's output can be confidently wrong, and a check for each.
qbank.answer: First, invented APIs, functions or flags: compile and run the code. Second, claiming tests passed without running them: re-run in CI. Third, special-casing tests, hard-coding expected values or editing the tests: diff the test files and use held-out inputs. Fourth, solving an easier problem than the one asked, silently dropping requirements: walk the acceptance criteria one by one. Others: stale knowledge of a library version, and changes outside the scope; limit the files it may touch.

qbank.question: What kinds of limits should an unattended agent run have?
qbank.answer: Resource limits: maximum turns, wall-clock time, tokens and money. Scope limits: which directories and repositories it may write, which network hosts it may reach, no production credentials. Action limits: no irreversible or outward-facing actions (force push, deleting, sending messages, deploying) without approval. Behaviour limits: stop if the same action repeats or the task grows beyond the brief. And a kill switch you can reach quickly, with logs of everything it did, so you can see and undo it.

qbank.question: An agent stuck in a loop makes a call every 20 seconds, each with a 100,000-token input at a hypothetical $3 per million input tokens. What does an unattended hour cost, and an 8-hour night?
qbank.answer: Calls per hour: 3,600 / 20 = 180. Input tokens: 180 x 100,000 = 18 million. Cost: 18 x $3 = $54 an hour. Over 8 hours it is $432, and that is only input. A cap of, say, 50 turns or $10 for the task stops it after about 17 minutes of looping instead. This is why you set limits before the run: the loop is silent and the cost accumulates faster than anyone checks.
checklist: A spend or turn cap stops it

qbank.question: Should the agent stop hard when it reaches a limit, or warn and continue?
qbank.answer: A hard stop guarantees the limit but can abandon a task that was close to done, leave half-finished edits, and train people to raise limits carelessly. A soft warning lets valuable work finish but can be ignored, especially when nobody is watching. Mix them: warn at about 70% of the budget so the agent can wrap up and write a status, hard stop at 100%, and leave the work in a clean state (a commit or branch with notes). Use hard limits for money and irreversible actions, soft ones for turns and time.

qbank.question: Design the guardrails for an agent that works overnight on a branch of a real repository.
qbank.answer: Run it in a sandbox with only that repository, no production credentials and a network allowlist. Give it a feature branch and permission to push only that branch; main is protected and merging needs a person. Set hard caps on turns, time and spend, with a warning at 70%. It commits small checkpoints and writes a progress file. Destructive commands are denied by rule. A watchdog stops it if there is no progress for 30 minutes. In the morning you get a report: what changed, what it ran, what failed and what it did not finish.

qbank.question: What is approval fatigue, and how does it weaken a human-in-the-loop design?
qbank.answer: If a person is asked to approve many small actions, nearly all of which are fine, they begin to click yes without reading. Then the approval step still exists on paper but gives no protection, and the one dangerous action gets through. Fix it by asking less and asking better: let safe, reversible actions run under a policy, ask only for risky or irreversible ones, show what will change in plain terms, and make the default safe. Measure how often you reject, because zero rejections suggests the gate is not working.

qbank.question: Review every action, or review the results with risk-based approval?
qbank.answer: Reviewing every action keeps control but removes most of the benefit of an agent and leads to fatigue. Reviewing only results is fast, but you may find a mistake after it has done damage. A risk-tiered scheme sits between: no review for reversible, low-impact actions inside a sandbox; review of the result for medium risk; approval before the action for irreversible, costly or outward-facing ones. Check the tiers against your incident log and move actions between tiers as you learn.

qbank.question: Write the escalation rules that tell an agent when it must stop and ask a person.
qbank.answer: Escalate when: the request is ambiguous in a way that changes the result; the task needs a decision about money, security, privacy, or public communication; the change would be irreversible or touch production; the plan has to leave the agreed scope or interface; checks fail repeatedly after a few attempts; or the agent finds something that contradicts the spec. The escalation message should state what it was doing, what it found, the options with a recommendation, and what it will do if nobody answers. It then waits rather than choosing silently.
checklist: Message with options and a default

qbank.question: What is drift between an agent's output and your intent, and how do you notice it early?
qbank.answer: Drift is the gradual move away from what you wanted: each step is plausible, but over a long task the agent adds extras, narrows the goal or follows its own earlier assumption. It is quiet because nothing fails. Notice it by comparing against the written spec at checkpoints, keeping diffs small and frequent, reading its plan notes rather than only the final result, sampling outputs, and watching rework rate over time. If the agent's summary no longer matches the spec, stop and re-anchor with a fresh session and the original brief.

qbank.question: The factory tracks cycle time, rework rate and cost per merged change. What does each one tell you, and what can each hide?
qbank.answer: Cycle time, from ticket to merged change, shows speed; it can hide poor quality if people rush merges. Rework rate, the share of changes that needed a follow-up fix or redo, shows quality of specs and gates; it can hide problems if rework is not recorded or if small changes are merged to look good. Cost per merged change shows efficiency; it can hide your own time if you count only API spend. Read the three together, since improving one by hurting another is easy.

qbank.question: In a month the factory merged 40 changes. Agent spend was $120, and you spent 10 hours reviewing and fixing, which you value at $50 an hour. Eight changes needed rework. What are the cost per merged change and the rework rate?
qbank.answer: Total cost is $120 + 10 x $50 = $620. Divided by 40 merged changes it is $15.50 per change. Counting only API spend would give $3 per change, which hides most of the cost. Rework rate is 8 / 40 = 20%. If each reworked change needed another hour of your time, that is part of the 10 hours. Compare with doing the same changes yourself to see whether the factory helps, not just whether it produces output.

qbank.question: Cycle time fell by half but rework rate doubled. Is the factory better?
qbank.answer: Not necessarily. Doubling the rework suggests the specs are weaker or the gates are catching less, so speed is being bought with later fixes. Net effect depends on cost: if a change now takes half the time but 40% instead of 20% need another pass, then total time per correct change may be about the same or worse, and the review burden on you rises. Look at time to a correct merge, including rework, and at whether defects escape to users. Then fix specs or gates before pushing speed further.
checklist: Specs or gates are the cause
Measure time to a correct merge

qbank.question: Design the pipeline from ticket to merged pull request for your side projects, with the gates you would put in.
qbank.answer: Ticket template with goal, constraints and acceptance criteria. An agent writes a plan, which you approve for anything larger than a small fix. Worker agents implement in separate branches or worktrees with spend caps. CI runs build, tests and lint; a second agent reviews the diff against the ticket; held-out checks run. A human reviews risky areas and merges. A log row per ticket records start and end time, spend, rework and cause. A weekly review of the three numbers decides what to tighten.

qbank.question: Explain latency, bandwidth and the bandwidth-delay product, and say why a long, fast link can still give slow transfers.
qbank.answer: Latency is how long one bit takes to get across; bandwidth is how many bits per second the link can carry. The bandwidth-delay product (bandwidth x round-trip time) is how much data must be in flight to keep the link full. TCP only has one window of unacknowledged data in flight at a time, so if the window is smaller than the product, the sender idles waiting for acknowledgements and throughput drops below the link speed. Larger windows, window scaling and parallel streams fix this.
checklist: TCP window limits data in flight
Sender idles when window is small

qbank.question: A 10 Gbit/s link has a 50 ms round-trip time. What is the bandwidth-delay product, and what throughput does a fixed 64 KiB window give?
qbank.answer: 10 Gbit/s is 1.25 GB/s; times 0.05 s gives 62.5 MB that must be in flight to fill the pipe. A 64 KiB (65,536 byte) window sends 65,536 bytes per round trip: 65,536 / 0.05 = 1.31 MB/s, or about 10.5 Mbit/s, roughly 0.1% of the link. Modern TCP uses window scaling and auto-tuning to grow the window, but buffers must be large enough. This is why copying large weights across regions can crawl on default settings.

qbank.question: A service streams tokens to 100,000 users at 50 tokens per second each, one small server-sent event of about 100 bytes per token. What bandwidth and event rate is that, and what does it mean for the design?
qbank.answer: Events per second: 100,000 x 50 = 5 million. Bytes: 5e6 x 100 = 500 MB/s, about 4 Gbit/s, before TCP and TLS overhead. The event rate matters as much as the bandwidth: millions of tiny writes per second cost CPU in syscalls, TLS and packet processing, so you batch several tokens per write when latency allows, keep connections on efficient proxies, and spread across many instances. Per-connection memory for 100,000 sockets also needs planning.

qbank.question: Server-sent events, WebSocket or gRPC streaming for delivering tokens to clients?
qbank.answer: Server-sent events are plain HTTP, one-way, easy to proxy and cache-bypass, and the browser reconnects for you; they fit text streaming. WebSocket is two-way and good for interactive or voice use, but needs its own handling of proxies, idle timeouts and scaling of long-lived connections. gRPC streaming is efficient between services with typed messages and flow control, but browsers need a gateway. All three hold a connection open, so check load balancer idle timeouts, HTTP/2 stream limits, and what happens to a reconnecting client mid-answer.

qbank.question: What happens when a container goes over its memory limit, and what happens when it goes over its CPU limit?
qbank.answer: Memory is incompressible. When a cgroup reaches its memory.max and the kernel cannot reclaim enough (for example by dropping cache), the OOM killer kills a process in that cgroup. CPU is compressible: with a quota the group is simply throttled, so its threads stop running until the next period. Memory overruns therefore appear as sudden kills, while CPU overruns appear as unexplained latency, with the throttling counters in the cgroup's cpu.stat rising.

qbank.question: A pod has a CPU limit of 2 cores (quota 200 ms per 100 ms period) and runs 8 busy threads. How long into each period does it get throttled, and how long does it stall?
qbank.answer: Eight busy threads consume 8 ms of CPU per millisecond of wall time. The quota of 200 ms is used up after 200 / 8 = 25 ms. The group is then throttled for the remaining 75 ms of the 100 ms period. So requests that arrive in that window wait up to 75 ms, which shows up as p99 latency even though average CPU use looks like exactly 2 cores. Fixes: raise the limit, reduce the thread count, or set a request without a limit.

qbank.question: What is eBPF, and why is it useful for observing a production host without changing the applications?
qbank.answer: eBPF lets you load small programs into the kernel, attached to hooks such as system calls, kernel functions, tracepoints and network events. A verifier checks each program before it runs so it cannot crash the kernel or loop forever. Programs write results into maps that user space reads. You can then count syscalls per container, trace TCP retransmits, measure disk latency or block a call, with low overhead and no change to the application or restart. Limits: needs a recent kernel and privilege, and programs are restricted.

qbank.question: For a GPU inference container, how would you set memory limits, and what is the risk of a limit that is too tight or too loose?
qbank.answer: Set the memory limit above the real peak (model loading, tokeniser, pinned host buffers, page cache of the weight files) with a margin, and set requests equal to what you expect to use. Too tight: the OOM killer ends the server during model load or a traffic spike, and the restart then repeats the slow weight load. Too loose or none: one pod can eat the node's memory and push neighbours to be killed. Remember that file cache counts toward the cgroup, so reading large weight files can raise usage. Test the peak by loading under the limit.
checklist: Too tight: OOM and slow restart

qbank.question: Where do a program's system calls go in a normal container, and where do they go under gVisor? What does that change about an attack?
qbank.answer: In a normal container the process makes system calls straight to the host Linux kernel, which is shared by every container; a kernel bug can let it escape. Under gVisor, the calls go to the Sentry, a kernel written in Go that runs in user space and handles most of them itself, calling the host with only a small, filtered set of its own. An attacker must first break the Sentry and then the small host interface, so the host kernel's attack surface is much smaller.
checklist: Few host calls from the Sentry

qbank.question: Design the comparison you will run in a container and in gVisor, so you can see the isolation difference for yourself.
qbank.answer: Run the same small test program in both. Probe what it can see and do: print uname -r and the kernel version, read /proc entries such as /proc/cpuinfo and /proc/kallsyms, list mounts, try dmesg, try to open /dev/mem, try to load a module or change time, try ptrace and unusual syscalls. Record each result as allowed, denied or different. Add a small benchmark of syscalls and file I/O to see the cost. Present as a table: operation, container result, gVisor result.

qbank.question: A program makes 200,000 system calls a second. Suppose each costs 1 microsecond natively and 5 microseconds under a sandbox. How much CPU does the syscall work take in each case? (Numbers are made up for the exercise; measure real ones.)
qbank.answer: Native: 200,000 x 1 microsecond = 0.2 seconds of CPU per second, so 20% of one core. In the sandbox: 200,000 x 5 microseconds = 1 second per second, a full core. The sandbox adds 0.8 core of work for the same program, and it would throttle a one-core limit. A compute-heavy program with few syscalls would see almost no difference. This is why isolation overhead depends on the workload, and why you benchmark your own.

qbank.question: What do you give up by choosing gVisor over a plain container?
qbank.answer: You gain a smaller attack surface, but pay with performance on syscall-heavy and file-heavy workloads (extra work in the Sentry), with compatibility, since not every syscall or kernel feature is implemented, and with some debugging tools that expect real kernel behaviour. Networking and some device access, including GPUs, need specific support. Pure compute code runs at nearly native speed. So choose it for untrusted code that is not extremely I/O-heavy, and test your actual workload on it first.

qbank.question: What hardening can you apply to a normal container, and why is it still not a strong boundary for untrusted code?
qbank.answer: You can drop Linux capabilities, run as a non-root user, use user namespaces, apply a seccomp profile to restrict system calls, use AppArmor or SELinux, make the filesystem read-only and limit resources with cgroups. These reduce what a process can do and which kernel code it can reach. But all containers still share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability reachable through any allowed syscall can break out. For untrusted or model-written code, add a stronger boundary such as gVisor or a microVM.

qbank.question: A host has 256 GiB of RAM. Each Firecracker microVM gets 512 MiB of guest memory plus about 5 MiB of VMM overhead (Firecracker's spec states at most 5 MiB for a small VM; it varies with the workload). How many fit if you reserve nothing for the host? How many in practice?
qbank.answer: Each VM needs about 517 MiB. 256 GiB is 262,144 MiB. 262,144 / 517 is about 507 VMs. In practice you reserve memory for the host kernel, the management agent and page tables, and you want headroom for bursts, so plan on perhaps 400 to 450. Memory overcommit or ballooning can raise the density if guests rarely use all their memory, at some risk. Other limits, such as CPU cores, usually bind first.

qbank.question: Pick an isolation technology for three jobs: your own CI builds, model-generated code from many customers, and GPU workloads.
qbank.answer: Your own CI builds: containers with hardening are usually enough; the code is yours and speed matters. Model-generated code from many customers: a microVM (Firecracker, Kata) for a separate kernel and a hardware-virtualisation boundary, or gVisor if you need density and the workload is compatible. GPU workloads: GPUs are hard to isolate in microVMs, as they need device passthrough; containers with the NVIDIA runtime are common, MIG gives hardware partitions of one GPU, and gVisor has some GPU support. Treat shared GPU memory between tenants as a risk to check.

qbank.question: Design a service that runs code written by an AI agent for many users, safely.
qbank.answer: One microVM (or gVisor sandbox) per session, started from a snapshot of a base image so it begins in well under a second. No credentials in the guest; secrets, when needed, are added by a proxy outside. Network off by default, or egress through an allowlisting proxy. CPU, memory, disk and process limits, plus a wall-clock timeout. An ephemeral filesystem destroyed at the end, with artefacts copied out through a narrow channel. Log commands and network attempts. Test with known escape and resource-abuse programs.

qbank.question: You open a large unfamiliar Rust or C++ project. In what order do you read it?
qbank.answer: Start with the README and build files (Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt) to learn the structure, dependencies and entry points. Find main and follow the start-up path at a high level. Read the central types and traits or classes before the functions that use them. Use the tests as examples of intended use. Then trace one concrete scenario end to end with a debugger or logging instead of reading everything. Keep notes of the module map as you go.

qbank.question: For a reader who knows Go, what do &, &mut, Box and Arc mean in Rust code?
qbank.answer: & is a shared, read-only borrow; &mut is an exclusive, writable borrow: the compiler allows either many readers or one writer, never both, which removes data races at compile time. Box puts a value on the heap with a single owner, like a pointer you own. Arc is an atomically reference-counted pointer for sharing ownership across threads; combine with Mutex for shared mutable data. There is no garbage collector: values are dropped when their owner goes out of scope.
checklist: No GC; drop at scope end

qbank.question: Rust, C++ or Go for a performance-sensitive infrastructure component such as a sandbox manager?
qbank.answer: Go is quick to write, has good concurrency and networking and strong cloud tooling, at the cost of a garbage collector (usually short pauses) and less control over memory layout. Rust gives memory safety without a GC and strong control, which suits security-sensitive and low-level code (Firecracker is Rust), but has a steeper learning curve and slower builds. C++ has the largest existing base, including many inference engines, but safety depends on discipline. For most control-plane code Go is enough; for hot paths and isolation boundaries Rust is attractive.
checklist: Rust: safety without GC, learning curve

qbank.question: Make a two-hour plan for finding out how Firecracker starts a microVM.
qbank.answer: Clone the repository and read the top-level docs and design notes first. Open Cargo.toml to see the workspace and the rust-vmm crates it uses (such as kvm-ioctls and vm-memory). Find the main binary and follow the path from command-line arguments through the API server to the code that creates the VM, sets guest memory, loads the kernel and starts vCPU threads. Mark where KVM ioctls are called. Run it with logging, and write a one-page map: components, threads, and the order of start-up steps.
checklist: Run it and write a map

qbank.question: What lifecycle states does a sandbox go through in sandboxd, and what must happen if the manager crashes in the middle?
qbank.answer: Typical states: Requested, Creating, Running, Stopping, Destroyed, and Failed. The manager records the state of each sandbox durably. If it crashes, a recovery pass on restart compares what it recorded with what actually exists (VMs, processes, network devices, disk images) and fixes the difference: finish creating, or destroy orphans. Without that reaper, leaked sandboxes accumulate and use up memory, addresses and disk.

qbank.question: Design the HTTP API of sandboxd for an agent harness.
qbank.answer: POST /sandboxes creates one, with image, CPU and memory limits, network policy and a time-to-live, and returns an id; use an idempotency key so a retry does not create a second one. POST /sandboxes/{id}/exec runs a command and streams stdout, stderr and the exit code, with its own timeout. PUT and GET on /files move artefacts in and out with size limits. DELETE destroys it. GET returns state and usage. Every sandbox has a hard TTL enforced by the manager, per-caller quotas, and an audit log of each call.

qbank.question: The agent harness requests 50 new sandboxes per second at peak and each takes 2 seconds to become ready. How many sandboxes are in the starting state at any moment, and how big should a warm pool be to hide the start-up?
qbank.answer: By Little's law, the number in the starting state is arrival rate x time in that state = 50 x 2 = 100. So at peak, 100 sandboxes are always being started. To hide the delay, keep a pool of ready sandboxes at least as large as the number consumed during a start-up time, 100, and refill it at 50 per second; a larger pool covers bursts above the average. Idle pool members cost memory, so size from measured peaks and let the pool shrink off-peak.
checklist: Little's law: L = lambda x W

qbank.question: Should sandboxd reuse a sandbox for the next task or always create a fresh one?
qbank.answer: Reuse saves start-up time and keeps caches (installed packages, built code) warm, but any leftover state can leak between tasks: files, environment variables, background processes, network connections and secrets. For tasks from the same user in one session that is often fine. Across users or untrusted tasks, always use a fresh sandbox, or restore from a clean snapshot, which gives almost the speed of reuse with a known state. Make the rule a policy tied to the trust boundary rather than a performance switch.

qbank.question: What are the common mistakes when benchmarking an LLM endpoint, and how do you avoid them?
qbank.answer: Measuring cold: the first requests include model loading, caches and compilation, so warm up and discard them. Using the average: latency is skewed, so report percentiles. Fixed identical prompts: they hit prefix caches and hide real behaviour, so use a realistic mix of lengths. Closed-loop load that slows when the server slows, hiding overload; use open-loop arrivals for capacity. Measuring only throughput: report TTFT and per-token latency against load. Running the client on the same box or a saturated network.

qbank.question: Roughly how many requests do you need for a stable p99, and why is p99.9 harder?
qbank.answer: The p99 is estimated from the slowest 1% of requests. With 1,000 requests, only 10 requests sit in the tail, so one outlier moves the estimate a lot. A common rule of thumb is to have at least 100 observations beyond the percentile, so about 10,000 requests for p99 and 100,000 for p99.9. Also measure for long enough to include periodic events such as garbage collection or autoscaling. Report confidence by repeating runs and showing the spread.
checklist: Rule of thumb 100 in the tail

qbank.question: Benchmark with synthetic fixed-length prompts or with replayed real traffic?
qbank.answer: Synthetic prompts are repeatable, easy to scale and let you vary one thing at a time (input length, output length, concurrency), which is ideal for finding the engine's limits. Real traces capture the true mix of lengths, shared prefixes, bursts and user behaviour, which decides the actual caching and queueing results, but contain private data, are harder to scale to future load and mix many effects together. Use synthetic tests to understand the system and replayed (scrubbed) traces to validate capacity for your own traffic.
checklist: Real: true mix and prefix sharing

qbank.question: Design a benchmark that finds the maximum goodput of an LLM endpoint for a stated latency target.
qbank.answer: Define the SLO first, for example p99 TTFT under 500 ms and p99 per-token latency under 50 ms. Build a workload with the input and output length distribution of your traffic. Drive it open-loop with Poisson arrivals, raising the request rate in steps, with a warm-up and a few minutes at each step. Record TTFT, per-token latency, errors and the fraction of requests meeting the SLO. Goodput is the rate of requests that met the target. Plot goodput against offered load and report the load at which it peaks, with repeats for variance.

qbank.question: For a single queue with one server, how does the mean time in the system change with utilisation, in multiples of the service time?
qbank.answer: For the simple M/M/1 model, mean time in system is service time / (1 - utilisation). At 50% utilisation it is 2 times the service time, at 80% it is 5 times, at 90% it is 10 times and at 95% it is 20 times. The curve is gentle at first and then rises steeply. The 99th percentile is worse still: the time in the system is exponentially distributed, so p99 is about 4.6 times the mean. That is why capacity planning leaves headroom.

qbank.question: An LLM service receives 50 requests per second and the mean time a request spends in the system is 4 seconds. How many requests are in the system on average? If each holds 300 MB of KV cache, how much memory is that?
qbank.answer: Little's law: L = arrival rate x time in system = 50 x 4 = 200 requests. At 300 MB each that is 200 x 300 MB = 60 GB of KV cache across the fleet on average. Peaks will be higher, so provision for the p99 concurrency, not the mean. Little's law holds for any stable system, with no assumption about distributions, which makes it useful to cross-check measurements: if your dashboards show a different number, a metric is wrong.

qbank.question: Eight servers each with their own queue, or one shared queue feeding all eight?
qbank.answer: A shared queue is better: a request waits only if all eight servers are busy, while with separate queues a request can be stuck after a long job on one server while another sits idle. At the same total load this pooling gives clearly lower waiting times and a thinner tail. Separate queues are simpler and avoid a central point, and are what you get with naive load balancing. Approximate pooling with smart routing (send to the least loaded or use power-of-two choices), and note that LLM output lengths vary widely, which makes the effect stronger.

qbank.question: Plan the capacity of a service whose p99 response time must stay under 20 times the mean service time. Use the M/M/1 estimate to find the utilisation ceiling, then say what else you add.
qbank.answer: For M/M/1 the response time is exponential with mean service / (1 - rho), so p99 is about 4.6 x service / (1 - rho). Setting 4.6 / (1 - rho) = 20 gives 1 - rho = 0.23, so rho = 77%. That is the ceiling for a single queue under this model. Real LLM service times vary more than exponential, so use load tests to find the real knee and set a lower ceiling, often 50 to 70%. Then add N+1 spare capacity for failures and headroom for autoscaler lag.
checklist: p99 = ln(100) x mean, about 4.6 x
Lower ceiling for heavy-tailed service times

qbank.question: What is the USE method, and how do you apply it to a slow server?
qbank.answer: USE stands for utilisation, saturation and errors. For each resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, and for GPUs compute, memory and links) you check how busy it is, whether work is queueing for it (run queue length, disk queue, retransmits), and whether it reports errors. It gives a systematic checklist so you do not guess. A resource with high utilisation or any saturation is a candidate bottleneck. Errors, such as dropped packets or ECC counts, are often quick wins. Then drill into the suspect with a profiler.

qbank.question: How do you read a flame graph, and what is the difference between on-CPU and off-CPU profiling?
qbank.answer: In a flame graph each box is a function; width is the fraction of samples where it was on the stack, and the stack grows upward from callers to callees. You look for wide boxes, especially wide plateaus at the top, since those are where time is spent. On-CPU profiles sample what the CPU is running, so they show where computation goes. Off-CPU profiles show where threads wait (locks, I/O, sleeps, network), which explains a slow request whose CPU use is low. You need both to tell working from waiting.

qbank.question: A request spends 40% of its time in step A. You make step A 2 times faster, and then 10 times faster. What is the overall speed-up in each case?
qbank.answer: Amdahl's law: speed-up = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / s), with f = 0.4. For s = 2: 1 / (0.6 + 0.2) = 1.25. For s = 10: 1 / (0.6 + 0.04) = 1.5625. Even an infinitely fast step A would give only 1 / 0.6 = 1.67. So you gain more by finding the largest part of the time than by heroic work on a small one, and after each fix, profile again because the shares change.

qbank.question: A request to your LLM service sometimes takes 12 seconds instead of 2. Design the investigation that tells you whether it was waiting or working.
qbank.answer: Start with a trace: split the request's time into spans for queueing, tokenisation, prefill, decode steps and post-processing. Compare wall time with CPU time for the slow request: low CPU suggests waiting. Check queue time and the number of running requests when it arrived, KV cache usage and preemptions, and GPU utilisation and clocks in the same window. Look for a long prompt or long output in the same batch, GC pauses, retries inside the client, or a cold replica. Reproduce with the same input at low load to separate the request from the system state.
checklist: Queue and KV state at arrival
Concurrent heavy requests, GC, retries, cold replicas

qbank.question: For an LLM service, what do you capture in metrics, logs and traces, and what is specific to LLMs?
qbank.answer: Metrics are cheap aggregates over time: request rate, errors, latency percentiles, tokens per second, queue depth. Logs are individual records with details. Traces follow one request through the services as timed spans. LLM-specific fields: model and version, prompt template version, input and output token counts, time to first token and per-token latency, stop reason, cost, cache hit, tool calls and their results, and a quality signal such as a judge score or user feedback. OpenTelemetry has draft conventions for generative AI spans.

qbank.question: Should you log full prompts and responses?
qbank.answer: Full text is what you need to debug a bad answer, build eval sets and replay problems. But it often contains personal or confidential data, increases storage cost, and creates a sensitive store that can be breached or subpoenaed. Alternatives: log metadata only (sizes, hashes, model, latency) by default; capture full text for a small sample, for errors, or when a user reports a problem and opts in; redact obvious personal data; set short retention; restrict access and audit reads. Decide with legal and security, not only engineering.

qbank.question: A service handles 1 million requests a day; each request plus response is about 3,000 tokens, roughly 12 KB of text. How much raw trace text per day, and for 90 days? What if you keep only 10%?
qbank.answer: 1,000,000 x 12 KB = 12 GB per day of raw text. Over 90 days that is 1.08 TB. Compression of text typically gives 3 to 5 times, so about 220 to 360 GB stored. Sampling 10% reduces it to 1.2 GB a day and about 108 GB for 90 days raw. Always keep errors and slow requests in the sample and sample the rest, so you retain what you need for debugging at a fraction of the cost.
checklist: Sample, but keep errors and slow

qbank.question: Design the trace for one multi-step agent task.
qbank.answer: One root span for the task with the user, task id, budget and final outcome. Child spans for each model call, with model, prompt version, token counts, TTFT, total time, stop reason and cost, and a span for each tool call with tool name, arguments (redacted), duration, result size and error. Link steps in order and mark retries. Add events for approvals and guardrail triggers. Sample all failed, slow or expensive tasks and a small share of others. Use the same ids in logs so you can pivot. Then build views: cost by step, slowest tools, loops.
checklist: Span per model call with tokens and cost

qbank.question: A GPU costs $3 per hour and serves 2,500 output tokens per second when saturated. What is the cost per million output tokens at full use, and at 30% average use?
qbank.answer: At full use: 2,500 x 3,600 = 9 million tokens per hour. $3 / 9 = $0.33 per million tokens. At 30% use the GPU produces 2.7 million tokens per hour for the same $3, so $3 / 2.7 = $1.11 per million, more than three times as much. The price of idle time is the main lever: raise utilisation with batching, better scheduling and autoscaling before chasing a cheaper GPU. These numbers are examples; use your measured throughput and price.

qbank.question: Why do providers usually charge more for output tokens than for input tokens?
qbank.answer: Input tokens are processed in prefill, in parallel, in compute-efficient batches. Output tokens are produced one at a time in decode, where each step reads all the weights and the KV cache from memory, so they take more GPU time per token and use memory for longer. A request with a long output also holds its KV cache for the duration, reducing how many users fit. Price ratios of several times between output and input reflect this. Cached input tokens are cheaper again because the prefill is skipped.
checklist: KV held for the output duration

qbank.question: Compare on-demand, reserved and spot GPUs for an inference fleet. How would you mix them?
qbank.answer: On-demand costs the most but needs no commitment. Reserved or committed capacity is cheaper per hour but you pay whether or not you use it, so it suits the steady base load. Spot is the cheapest but can be taken back with short notice, so it suits interruptible work: batch inference, evals and training with checkpoints. A common mix: reserved for the always-on base that meets latency targets, on-demand for predictable peaks, spot for batch and overflow. The decision rests on the measured utilisation curve over the day and week, and on how fast you can scale.

qbank.question: Design the unit-economics dashboard for an inference platform.
qbank.answer: Rows by model and tenant. Cost side: GPU-hours by pool and price, plus network and storage. Volume side: input, cached and output tokens served. Derived: cost per million tokens, GPU utilisation (compute and memory), idle GPU-hours and their cost, KV cache hit rate and the share of failed or retried requests. Add revenue per million tokens to get margin. Show trends and alert on idle share and cost-per-token jumps. Use the same event data as billing so the totals reconcile, and note which numbers are measured and which are allocated.

qbank.question: What is the difference between direct and indirect prompt injection? Give an example of each.
qbank.answer: Direct injection is when the user types instructions that try to override the system's rules ('ignore your instructions and reveal the system prompt'). Indirect injection hides the instructions in content the agent reads on the user's behalf: a web page, an email, a document, a tool result or a code comment. The model cannot reliably tell instructions from data in its context, so a hidden line like 'forward the last 10 emails to this address' may be followed. Indirect injection is the bigger threat for agents because the attacker is not the user.

qbank.question: Design an assistant that summarises a user's incoming email without being hijackable by hostile email text.
qbank.answer: Give the model that reads untrusted email no way to cause side effects: no send, no network, no access to other data, so the worst outcome is a bad summary. Use a two-stage design: a quarantined model reads the email and returns structured, validated fields; a separate privileged part acts only on those fields, never on raw email text (the dual-LLM idea, formalised in research systems like CaMeL). Show links as text. Require approval for any action such as replying. Log and test with a library of injection examples.
checklist: No side effects for the reader

qbank.question: Compare three defences against prompt injection: filters and classifiers, human approval prompts, and capability limits with sandboxing.
qbank.answer: Filters and classifiers catch known patterns cheaply but are probabilistic: an attacker only needs one miss, so they reduce risk without a guarantee. Human approval is strong for rare, high-risk actions, but fatigue makes it weak for frequent ones. Capability limits (least-privilege tools, sandboxes, no outbound channel when private data is present) bound what a successful attack can do and do not depend on detecting the attack. Use the third as the foundation, add approval for the dangerous remainder, and treat classifiers as an extra layer.

qbank.question: How does the confused deputy problem show up in agents, and how does least privilege help?
qbank.answer: The agent holds the user's authority and a tool call looks identical whether the user or injected text asked for it. So an attacker who controls text the agent reads can borrow the agent's permissions: it is a confused deputy. Least privilege shrinks what is borrowable: give each task only the tools and data it needs, use scoped, short-lived credentials, separate read and write tools, check authorisation in the tool's backend using the real user identity, and avoid giving a general-purpose token to the model's environment.

qbank.question: List the main ways model weights can be lost or stolen, and name one control for each.
qbank.answer: Insider copying: restrict and log access, require approval for export. Compromised credentials or accounts: strong authentication, short-lived credentials, least privilege. Theft from storage or backups: encryption at rest with keys held separately, controlled backups. Network exfiltration: egress controls and volume alerts. Supply-chain or malicious dependencies in the training or serving stack: signed artefacts, pinned dependencies, isolation. Theft through the API by querying to copy behaviour (distillation): rate limits and abuse monitoring, which reduce but cannot remove it.

qbank.question: A 70B model in bf16 is about 140 GB. How long does it take to copy out over a 1 Gbit/s uplink and over 10 Gbit/s? What egress alert threshold would catch it?
qbank.answer: At 1 Gbit/s (0.125 GB/s): 140 / 0.125 = 1,120 seconds, about 19 minutes. At 10 Gbit/s (1.25 GB/s): 112 seconds. So an exfiltration can finish in minutes, and a daily log review is too slow. An alert should fire on sustained or total outbound volume from weight-storage and serving nodes well below the model size, for example a few GB in an hour from hosts that normally send almost nothing, plus a hard egress allowlist so such a transfer is blocked at all.
checklist: Review must be near real time
Alert on volume from weight hosts

qbank.question: How far should you go with encryption and hardware protection of weights in use, such as confidential computing, and what does it cost?
qbank.answer: Weights must be in plain form in GPU memory to run, so encryption at rest and in transit protects storage and networks but not a compromised host. Confidential computing on CPUs and, on newer GPUs, trusted execution modes protect data in use from the host operator, which helps against a malicious or compromised infrastructure layer. Costs: some performance overhead, newer and more limited hardware, harder operations and debugging, and attestation to build. The RAND report links the level of protection to the capabilities of the attacker you must resist, so decide from your threat model.
checklist: At rest and in transit vs in use

qbank.question: Design access controls for the storage that holds model weights.
qbank.answer: Keep weights in a dedicated bucket or volume in an isolated account, with encryption by a key in a key management service that few can use. Serving nodes get read access through short-lived, role-based credentials bound to the node identity, not to people. People have no standing access; export or copy needs a time-limited request with a second person's approval. Log every read with who, what and bytes, and alert on unusual volumes or new readers. Restrict egress from the storage network. Add integrity hashes so tampering is detected, and test restore from backup.
checklist: No standing human access; two-person export

qbank.question: Why are two runs of the same model on the same eval not always identical even at temperature 0, and how do you make results comparable?
qbank.answer: Even with greedy decoding, results can differ because of floating-point non-associativity: the order in which operations are summed changes with batch size, kernel choice and hardware, so a tiny difference can flip a near-tie token and change the rest of the answer. Provider-side changes, such as a different model snapshot, add more. To compare: pin the model version, settings, prompts and eval code, run several samples per item and report the mean and interval, and record hardware and software versions. Treat differences smaller than the run-to-run spread as noise.

qbank.question: A safety eval finds 0 harmful outputs in 1,000 prompts. What is the upper bound on the true rate, with 95% confidence?
qbank.answer: With zero events observed in n trials, the 95% upper bound on the rate is about 3 / n (the rule of three). Here 3 / 1,000 = 0.3%. So you cannot claim the rate is zero; you can say it is probably below 0.3%. To support a claim of under 0.01% you need about 30,000 prompts without a single failure. Rare risks need big sets or targeted adversarial prompts, and the bound only covers the kind of prompts you sampled.
checklist: Zero events is not zero risk
Bound covers only the sampled distribution

qbank.question: Run safety evals at every training checkpoint, or only on release candidates?
qbank.answer: Every checkpoint gives early warning and a trend, so you can see when a capability or risk appears and stop a bad run. It costs compute and infrastructure time, especially for agentic evals that need sandboxes. Release-candidate-only is cheap but you learn late, when changing course is expensive.
